  • Recent findings suggest that the launch adds a second routing tier above the existing SageMaker HyperPod Inference Gateway.
  • AWS is addressing a capacity-utilization problem: requests can queue on a saturated cluster while already-provisioned GPUs sit idle elsewhere.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AWS introduced Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Global Inference Gateway on November 20, 2026, giving customers one managed endpoint for inference requests across registered HyperPod clusters in a single AWS Region or multiple Regions. The service selects a cluster using capacity, queue, proximity and error signals, with automatic failover when a cluster becomes unavailable.

Recent findings suggest that the launch adds a second routing tier above the existing SageMaker HyperPod Inference Gateway. That cluster-level gateway continues to select individual model pods using signals including key-value (KV) cache utilization and queue depth; the upcoming global tier selects the cluster first, while leaving pod selection unchanged.

AWS is addressing a capacity-utilization problem: requests can queue on a saturated cluster while already-provisioned GPUs sit idle elsewhere. In its example of four models served across five clusters in two Regions, per-model serving requires clients to track 20 endpoints. Cluster-level gateways cut that to five, while the global gateway provides one. The managed tier removes the need to build and maintain load balancers, DNS and cross-Region networking for this routing, and lets peak traffic overflow to clusters with available capacity.

An operator publishes each participating cluster by enabling spec.globalRouting in its existing InferenceGatewayConfig, then calls CreateGlobalInferenceGateway with the clusters to group. Publishing creates a Network Load Balancer, a virtual private cloud (VPC) endpoint service and certificate resources in the customer’s account. An unpublished cluster cannot be added successfully.

Clients send OpenAI-compatible requests signed with AWS Signature Version 4 (SigV4) to the regional endpoint. The gateway authenticates the caller and selects a healthy cluster, AWS PrivateLink carries the request within or across Regions, and the cluster’s Inference Gateway chooses the model pod. SageMaker operates the routing fleet, private endpoints, certificate validation, health checks, authentication and rate limiting; a service-managed publisher on each cluster supplies load metrics.

For each request, the gateway scores healthy clusters using four configurable signals:.

Recent findings suggest that customers overriding the defaults must set all four weights, using values from 0.0 to 1.0 that total 1.0, and can disable a signal with zero. UpdateGlobalInferenceGateway changes the weighting for latest requests without reprovisioning, while in-flight requests finish under the old settings. AWS claims workloads that prioritize resilience over proximity can raise ErrorRate and lower RegionProximity.

The gateway health-checks every cluster and shifts traffic to the next-best cluster after a failure without requiring client changes, bringing a recovered cluster back gradually. A failed request is retried once on another cluster unless streaming has started; if no healthy cluster remains, the gateway returns HTTP 503. Adding a healthy cluster does not change the endpoint or disrupt other clusters, while removing one stops new requests but lets in-flight work finish.

It has been revealed that IAM separately controls standard and streaming invocation, and customer JSON Web Tokens, when used, travel inside the SigV4 signature. Requests reach clusters only over AWS PrivateLink, and AWS states that the gateway does not log or store prompts or completions. Deleting the global gateway stops its endpoint but leaves the per-cluster endpoints serving.

Recent findings suggest that bagelcode VP of AI Platform Jinhyung Park said in AWS’s announcement that beta tests routed requests across two Regions through the gateway and continued serving them when one cluster could no longer serve the model. That gave the company’s small platform team cross-Region failover without building or maintaining its own routing layer.

The service is available in 13 Regions: US East (N. Virginia and Ohio), US West (N. California and Oregon), South America (São Paulo), Europe (Frankfurt, Ireland, London and Stockholm), and Asia Pacific (Tokyo, Mumbai, Singapore and Sydney).

AWS advises single-cluster customers to remain on the cluster Inference Gateway endpoint and adopt the global service when adding a second cluster. Existing per-cluster endpoints continue serving during client migration, and a gateway containing only clusters in one Region can keep a workload there. A published cluster left outside any gateway receives no traffic even though its Network Load Balancer continues to run and incur charges.

By putting proximity, capacity and failure signals in one policy, the service makes the use of otherwise idle GPU capacity a configuration decision rather than a separate networking project.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that it's been fantastic to see the community dive into our new MiniMax M2, with many highlighting its impressive skills in complex agentic tasks. This is particularly exciting for me, as my work was centered on the agent alignment part of its post-training. In this post, I'd like to share some of the key insights and lessons we learned during that process.

If you've worked with LLM Agents, you've felt this pain: the same model can feel brilliant in one framework and useless in another. An agent might crush a tool-use leaderboard but fail spectacularly at a simple, real-world task. This gap between benchmark performance and practical usability is one of the biggest challenges in the field.

When we designed M2, we knew we had to tackle this problem head-on. This led us to two core, and sometimes conflicting, objectives:.

Recent findings suggest that so, who do we align with? The answer is both. We align with benchmarks to build skill, but we must ultimately align with the user by ensuring those skills work everywhere.

While the methods for acing benchmarks are a deep topic for another day, I want to focus on that second, trickier objective: How do we train an agent for the wild?

Early in the project, we hit a frustrating wall. Agent performance was inconsistent, and we struggled to diagnose why. After many discussions, especially with Professor @Junxian He and @Wenhu Chen, we arrived at our first major conclusion: Agents require Interleaved Thinking.

Recent findings suggest that this means that an agent's internal monologue—its "thinking"—can and should happen at any point during a task, not just once at the beginning like a standard reasoning model. This design is critical for two reasons:.

This principle became a cornerstone of M2's effectiveness.

It has been revealed that pro Tip for M2 Customers: Because M2 relies on Interleaved Thinking, its context is its memory. For best performance, you must retain the full session history, including the thinking steps. We've noticed that much of the community feedback about performance gaps stems from accidentally discarding this vital context, which is a common practice with simpler reasoning models.

Our initial theory was simple: tool scaling is agent generalization.

According to recent reports, we started with a minimal set of tools (a Python interpreter, search engine, a browser) to build a baseline of tool-calling capability. The roadmap was clear: scale up the number and variety of tools, and the agent's ability to generalize to unseen tools would naturally follow.

Industry observers note that at first, this worked. Our benchmark scores climbed to respectable levels. But as we dug deeper, we realized we were solving the wrong problem. The model aced the tests, but if we changed the environment even slightly—like swapping to a different scaffolding framework—its performance would plummet. We were still far from our goal of a "practically useful" model.

This led to our second, more profound realization: Agent generalization is not just about adapting to new tools; it's about adapting to perturbations across the model's entire operational space.

In a recent development, this sounds abstract, so let's break it down. Think about everything that can change in a single agent task:.

It has been revealed that our work on M2 taught us an immense amount about agents, generalization, and data, but it has opened up more questions than it answered. Many of our ideas are still on the whiteboard. In the coming months, we will be exploring these frontiers even more deeply, and we can't wait to bring you the next generation of powerful and genuinely useful models.

According to recent reports, is this the reason I observe output degradation in subsequent rounds in Chatbox+M2 API? Questions answered correctly in the first turn sometimes become incorrect.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • From the dotcom bubble to 200,00 cores of raw power.
  • Web hosting might seem like an unlikely on-ramp to supercomputer administration, but it set Mark O'Shea on his way to running some of Australia's most powerful machines.
  • O'Shea is team leader for supercomputing operations and senior supercomputing systems administrator at Australia's Pawsey Supercomputing Research Centre.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From the dotcom bubble to 200,00 cores of raw power.

Web hosting might seem like an unlikely on-ramp to supercomputer administration, but it set Mark O'Shea on his way to running some of Australia's most powerful machines.

O'Shea is team leader for supercomputing operations and senior supercomputing systems administrator at Australia's Pawsey Supercomputing Research Centre.

Pawsey is home to Setonix, an HPE Cray EX supercomputer with more than 200,000 AMD EPYC CPU cores and hundreds of AMD Instinct MI250X accelerators. Its GPU partition ranks 87th in the November TOP500 and 37th in the Green500, which measures computational performance per watt.

Industry observers note that "Working in web hosting wasn't much different to what I was doing a few years later with supercomputers," O'Shea tells The Register. "Datacenters are essentially several thousand computers, as are supercomputers.

"So, we essentially had the same problems," he indicates, especially as regards cooling and power management.

There's no single formal route into supercomputer administration in Australia, O'Shea indicates. He picked up the necessary skills over time.

Andrew Underwood, Dell's chief technology officer for high-performance computing and artificial intelligence across the Asia-Pacific, Japan, and China, says that lack of formal training means some supercomputer admins start in academia.

He's observed that many HPC admins emerge from the sciences, catching the computing bug during their studies. A biologist working with a massive genomics database, for example, might discover a taste for running the systems behind it.

"The biologist might decide they want to be someone working in IT helping other biologists transform their industry," Underwood indicates.

"One of the things I really admire about people who work in the supercomputing field is they take it so seriously," Underwood adds. "It's almost a passion, a hobby, more so than it is a job.".

"They want to play that real supporting and foundational role of assisting and engaging with scientists to help them use the technology to solve the problems the world faces.".

Recent findings suggest that O'Shea agrees, noting that many people who get into supercomputer admin are PhD graduates who stick around their universities after they graduate. Some of them gravitate toward running the departmental computers and then wind up in supercomputing.

"There are many roles around universities allowing people to be introduced to [supercomputer administration] while still doing enterprise-style or more departmental admin for researchers and system administration," O'Shea notes.

Regardless of how a supercomputer admin gets their gig, both O'Shea and Underwood say the supersysadmin community is tight knit – which may not always be a good thing.

"As an industry in supercomputing, we need to be open to people from diverse backgrounds," Underwood says, "and we need to build these frameworks like the Student Cluster Competition, conferences like eResearch and the SC Conference, where students can get educated and systems admins get exposed to continual training.".

Back at Pawsey, O'Shea notes that while the supercomputer systems admin job is interesting and challenging, there's one thing that always gives Setonix's admins a kick: seeing what scientists achieve with the machine.

One early highlight, O'Shea says, was producing a detailed image of a supernova remnant, crunching through a 43 TB dataset in the process.

According to recent reports, "It's an exciting place to be. But everyone on my team really loves it when we hear what the researchers are doing with the supercomputers. It's very motivating when the guys get to see the end results." ®.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Amazon Web Services launched managed cluster extensions for Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Slurm on November 20, 2026, bringing declarative configuration to software on running nodes through APIs or the SageMaker AI console.
  • Sources indicate that the launch addresses the part of a shared AI training cluster that changes after provisioning.
  • Administrators can install, configure, patch and remove the AWS-managed packages through the console, AWS CLI or an SDK.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Amazon Web Services launched managed cluster extensions for Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Slurm on November 20, 2026, bringing declarative configuration to software on running nodes through APIs or the SageMaker AI console. The first two extensions cover observability and user management, including directory integration.

Sources indicate that the launch addresses the part of a shared AI training cluster that changes after provisioning. HyperPod had already added API-driven Slurm configuration, AMI-based node setup, continuous provisioning, automatic topology management and deep health checks during 2026. Those features manage the cluster’s definition, capacity, network layout and hardware health; cluster extensions apply the same approach to node software that changes as research teams, monitoring requirements and package versions evolve.

Administrators can install, configure, patch and remove the AWS-managed packages through the console, AWS CLI or an SDK. HyperPod validates settings against the selected extension version’s schema before rollout and records the requested version and settings as the desired state. A node agent then applies only the components required by each node’s role, including on nodes added through scaling or replacement.

According to recent reports, updates submit only the settings being changed. HyperPod merges them into the stored configuration and restarts only affected components, without replacing nodes or rerunning lifecycle scripts. Fresh extension versions can also be installed without an AMI enhancement. HyperPod checks the stored settings against the new version’s schema before rollout, and upgrades only move forward.

Recent findings suggest that each extension reports Creating or Updating during rollout, Active when every node runs the requested configuration without a reported problem, and Degraded when nodes fail or report problems. DescribeClusterExtension groups node-level health complications by cause with a code, message and affected-node count. HyperPod retries internal failures; administrators can correct other causes and retry affected nodes with an revision call containing no configuration changes.

The sagemaker-observability extension collects node, GPU, Elastic Fabric Adapter, Slurm job and Slurm cluster metrics, sending them to Amazon CloudWatch or Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus. Metric categories, levels and collection intervals are configurable, while nodes run only role-relevant components, such as DCGM and EFA exporters on GPU nodes and Slurm cluster metrics on the controller.

An optional Amazon Managed Grafana workspace adds pre-created Clusters and Jobs dashboards. They connect cluster-wide health and Slurm state with per-node infrastructure metrics and resource use for individual jobs, including CPU, memory, GPU utilization, disk I/O and NCCL data.

The sagemaker-user-management extension creates Linux users and groups with consistent IDs across nodes, controls SSH and passwordless sudo access by node type, and registers users with Slurm accounting. Accounts can be declared locally, drawn from Active Directory over LDAPS, or both, including connections to AWS Directory Service for Microsoft Active Directory. New and replacement nodes receive the same configuration, and administrators can review access through the API instead of signing into each node.

Recent findings suggest that cluster extensions require a HyperPod Slurm cluster using the November 2, 2026 HyperPod AMI or later, with continuous provisioning enabled. Because extensions run software as root, AWS treats create, update and delete permissions as administrator permissions and advises against granting them to the cluster execution role. That role still needs access to metric destinations and Active Directory secrets, while user management requires a shared file system for home directories. Separate extension ARNs allow platform and monitoring teams to own different extensions.

Existing clusters can migrate one capability at a time while scripts and extensions coexist. The process requires updating the cluster software, disabling that capability in lifecycle scripts, manually removing script-installed agents during a maintenance window, and creating the extension on the clean cluster. Each component needs one owner: managing the same exporter, user or service through both mechanisms can cause installation or runtime conflicts. Custom AMIs and lifecycle scripts remain available for organization-specific software, and administrators retain SSH and direct configuration access to every node, including the controller.

Industry observers note that both extensions are available in all Regions where SageMaker HyperPod is supported. There is no additional charge for cluster extensions, but customers pay for underlying resources such as CloudWatch, Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus and AWS Secrets Manager.

For shared foundation-model clusters, the operational consequence is that common node software becomes a declared, continuously checked part of cluster state rather than a collection of provisioning scripts. Removing script-installed agents is the one manual fleet-wide migration step; afterward, scale-ups and replacement nodes inherit the same extension settings, while organization-specific tooling remains under the cluster team’s control.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News AWS Lambda Now Runs GPU Inference with 48 Concurrent Invocations Sharing One Model per GPU.

Nov 22, 2026 4 min read.

AWS has added GPU support to AWS Lambda: Event Functions running on Lambda Managed Instances can now run on EC2 G-series instances (G4dn, G5, G6, G6f, Gr6, Gr6f and G6e at launch), deployed as container images, and triggered by the same event sources as any other function. The feature is generally available in the commercial regions where both Managed Instances and G-series instances exist. It is priced at the EC2 On-Demand rate plus a 9.75 percent management fee and the standard $0.20 per million requests.

Sources indicate that as InfoQ reported last December, Managed Instances let a function run on EC2 capacity the customer selects and pays for, with Lambda handling provisioning, patching and scaling and several invocations sharing one execution environment. GPUs were missing at that launch. Daniel Abib, senior specialist solutions architect at AWS, describes the operator's side of the change:.

Industry observers note that you build an OCI image, point the function at it, and let Lambda handle provisioning, scaling, and event integration. There are no GPU drivers, CUDA versions, or AMIs to reconcile, and no clusters or device plugins to operate.

A capacity provider lists the allowed instance types, the VPC and a vCPU ceiling; Lambda picks the newest generation with capacity and falls back to older generations when newer ones are short:.

The function declares its GPU memory through a upcoming AcceleratorConfig block, next to memory, timeout, storage, and a per-environment concurrency:.

Concurrent invocations in one environment share a single copy of the model in GPU memory, up to 48 per environment, and scaling follows GPU utilization, CPU utilization, and concurrency. Publishing a version provisions the environments, downloads the weights, and warms the engine before the first event arrives; Seekable OCI lazy loading can cut environment start time by up to 70 percent.

It has been revealed that AWS ships five GPU base images: CUDA only, CuPy, PyTorch, vLLM, and SGLang. The two inference servers need no handler code; a MODEL_ID variable points to a Hugging Face or ModelScope repository, an S3 prefix, or a local path, and a model swap is a configuration change followed by a new version:.

Industry observers note that the limits are in the launch post: container images up to 32 GB, 32 GB of ephemeral storage, 2 to 32 GB of memory, 3 to 48 GB of accelerator memory, 15,000 vCPUs per capacity provider, and a timeout of up to 90 minutes for asynchronous and event source mapping invocations. Abib draws the line against the competition in one sentence: serverless GPU services that hide the same work "often sit outside your AWS environment, with no native event sources, identity, or networking.".

It has been revealed that the first hands-on reports came within a day. Classmethod's Akaike, who had corrected a conference talk in December after finding that no G-type was accepted, tried every accelerated instance type in us-east-1 and found 37 of 81 accepted, all G-family; P-family, G7, Inferentia, Trainium, and the Graviton-based g5g were refused, as were zip packages. A PyTorch benchmark ran about 66 times faster on the L4 than on the instance's CPU. Still, neither Terraform nor the Cloud Control provider knew AcceleratorConfig yet, and the GPU vCPU quota in a fresh account is zero: "if you use g6.xlarge (4 vCPU) with the default three instances, you need a quota of 12 vCPUs." A Terraform provider glitch and pull request, opened on 16 November by a user named sasidhar-aws, and a pull request from the same user remain open.

Sources indicate that A second test, by an AWS Community Builder writing as xbill, put Gemma 4 E2B on a single g6.2xlarge through the vLLM image, with Google's 4-bit QAT weights and a speculative-decoding drafter baked into a 9 GB image. One environment served all 48 simultaneous requests and every one of 417 calls succeeded, at roughly 130 tokens a second for a single request and 3,400 to 3,600 at 48. The friction was in the pipeline rather than the GPU: 484 seconds from publish to an active version, a Docker image index that Lambda rejected until it was pushed as a single-platform manifest, and a handler that returns complete replies, so time to first token could not be measured. His verdict keeps to that scope:.

According to recent reports, for a model behind events, queues or other AWS services, the Lambda GPU function is the simpler road: one image, one function, and Lambda keeps the server alive and routes the requests. Keep the drafter on for a chat with a few customers at a time, and publish without it for heavy batch load.

When streamed replies or full control of the server are needed, he writes, "run vLLM on an EC2 G6 yourself.".

The pricing model is the one Managed Instances introduced, with a lower fee for GPUs than the 15 percent charged on CPU instance types. Savings Aims and Reserved Instances apply to the instance, and there is no duration charge, so an instance bills for as long as the minimum environment count is above zero. Yan Cui's December analysis of the model, written when it still carried the line "GPU instances are NOT supported," applies to the GPU case unchanged:.

It has been revealed that regular Lambda functions can scale rapidly by tapping into a large, shared pool of EC2 instances. With managed instances, it takes tens of seconds to launch latest EC2 instances. As such, it's not a good fit when you have large, unpredictable spikes in traffic.

Managed Instances still support only Event Functions, so the GPU path does not yet reach Web Functions, the HTTP-server shape Lambda gained this year, and AWS has not stated whether it will.

  • Recent findings suggest that open-weight models have trained parameters that can be downloaded, run, and modified independently of the original developer, allowing derivatives to spread without a continuing commercial relationship.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anysphere, the developer of the Cursor AI coding platform, told House investigators it aims to explore phasing out Chinese-developed open-weight AI models because of geopolitical risk, according to a joint congressional report released November 20, 2026.

In a recent development, the disclosure is an exploratory proposal, not a completed phase-out, and the committees described no final decision or timetable. The House Committee on Homeland Security and the House Select Committee on China published the findings after an investigation that began in April 2026 and expanded from Airbnb and Anysphere to DoorDash on July 31, 2026.

Recent findings suggest that open-weight models have trained parameters that can be downloaded, run, and modified independently of the original developer, allowing derivatives to spread without a continuing commercial relationship. The committees mentioned Composer 2, Cursor’s flagship proprietary model, was built on a Moonshot AI base whose identity became public only after an independent developer identified it.

In a recent development, cursor’s technical report identifies that base as Kimi K2.5. Composer 2 underwent continued pretraining on a code-heavy data mix, followed by large-scale reinforcement learning in realistic Cursor sessions using the same tools and harness as the deployed model.

Recent findings suggest that airbnb reported that customized versions of Alibaba’s Qwen models support an AI assistant handling roughly 80,000 guest and host interactions daily, alongside a fine-tuned model summarizing roughly 250,000 support cases and calls each day. Both run on U.S.-based service-provider infrastructure.

According to recent reports, doorDash reported 25 Chinese model families authorized and deployed in a non-trivial manner, defined as incurring at least $5,000 in computing and serving costs. It estimated that replacing one Chinese-developed model embedded in a larger system could take up to six months, although most other uses could transition almost immediately.

The committees identified cost, customization, and near-frontier performance as adoption drivers, and found that the United States lacks a competitive open-weight alternative at the price and performance the market demands.

The report compares published API prices for one million input tokens and one million output tokens (small pieces of words and characters used to measure model usage):.

According to recent reports, those figures do not adjust for differences in capability, caching, batch discounts, promotions, or self-hosting costs. They illustrate the price pressure behind adoption, while open weights also let companies fine-tune models on their own data and deploy them on infrastructure they control.

The security concern is separate from hosting location. Running models on U.S. infrastructure reduces direct data exposure, but the report says that does not change how the underlying model was trained or how it may behave under conditions ordinary evaluations miss.

The report’s 12 recommendations do not themselves enact restrictions. They would build on a Department of Homeland Security order excluding DeepSeek products and services from federal civilian procurement and requiring their removal from agency systems, including third-party products built on DeepSeek. The chairmen recommend extending those restrictions to other Chinese-developed models and their derivatives across federal information systems and federal contract work, with narrow waivers for research, testing, and defensive security. They also recommend barring those models and derivatives from narrowly defined high-risk critical-infrastructure functions, with removal schedules tied to trusted alternatives and temporary exceptions where no trusted substitute exists.

To make the rules enforceable, a model-provenance standard led by the National Institute of Standards and Technology and a machine-readable AI bill of materials would document base models, significant fine-tuning, and distillation sources. The requirement would cover federal contractors and AI used in high-risk critical-infrastructure functions, and would be voluntary elsewhere. A national American open-weight AI initiative would combine public computing resources, shared evaluation infrastructure, voluntary licensing of American frontier-model outputs to qualified open-weight developers for training, and federal anchor demand.

The committees warn that removing Chinese models before trusted open-weight alternatives exist could raise costs and concentrate the market among closed proprietary providers. Anysphere’s exploratory strategy therefore illustrates the larger implementation test: restrictions need reliable lineage records to locate embedded models and credible substitutes to avoid trading Chinese open weights for higher costs or closed-model dependence.

Today, we are happy to announce a upcoming and deeper partnership with Google Cloud, to enable companies to build their own AI with open models.

“Google has made some of the most impactful contributions to open AI, from the OG transformer to the Gemma models. I believe in a future where all companies will build and customize their own AI. Salva, Senior Director of Product Management at Google Cloud. “Together we will make Google Cloud the best place to build with open models.”.

Industry observers note that google Cloud customers use open models from Hugging Face in many of its leading AI services. In Vertex AI, the most popular open models are ready to deploy in a couple clicks within Model Garden. Customers who want greater control over their AI infrastructure can find a similar model library available in GKE AI/ML, or use pre-configured environments maintained by Hugging Face. Customers also run AI inference workloads with Cloud Run GPUs, enabling serverless open model deployments.

The common thread: we work with Google Cloud to build seamless experiences fully leveraging the unique capabilities of each service to offer choice to the customers.

Usage of Hugging Face by Google Cloud customers has grown 10x over the last 3 years, and today, this translates into tens of petabytes of model downloads every month, in billions of requests.

To make sure Google Cloud customers have the best experience building with models and datasets from Hugging Face, we are working together to create a CDN Gateway for Hugging Face repositories built on top of both Hugging Face Xet optimized storage and data transfer technologies, and Google Cloud advanced storage and networking capabilities.

It has been revealed that this CDN Gateway will cache Hugging Face models and datasets directly on Google Cloud to significantly reduce downloading times, and strengthen model supply chain robustness for Google Cloud customers. Whether you’re using Vertex, GKE, Cloud Run or just building your own stack in VMs in Compute Engine, you will benefit from faster time-to-first-token and simplified model governance.

Sources indicate that hugging Face Inference Endpoints is the easiest way to go from model to deployment in just a couple clicks. Through this deepened partnership we will bring the unique capabilities and cost performance of Google Cloud to Hugging Face customers, starting with Inference Endpoints. Expect more and newer instances available as well as price drops!

It has been revealed that we will ensure all the fruits of our product and engineering collaboration become easily available to the 10 million AI Builders on Hugging Face. Going from a model page to deploying on Vertex Model Garden or GKE should only take a couple steps. Taking a private model securely hosted in an Enterprise organization on Hugging Face should be as easy as working with public models.

We want to make sure Hugging Face owners can fully benefit from the current and the next generations of TPUs when they build AI with open models. We are excited to make TPUs as easy to use as GPUs for Hugging Face models, thanks to native support in our libraries.

We are excited to make this future happen with Google Cloud. Our deep collaboration will accelerate this vision, whether you are using Vertex AI Model Garden, Google Kubernetes Engine, Cloud Run or Hugging Face Inference Endpoints.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Kit piggybacks off TV and mobile signals and can be neatly stuffed into an SUV.

BAE Systems is developing a passive radar system it claims could track airborne threats at a fraction of the cost of conventional radar, using existing broadcasts rather than transmitting signals that could reveal its position.

Recent findings suggest that the defense biz says its covert radar technology detects reflections of television, radio, and mobile network transmissions from airborne objects. That lets it monitor airspace without broadcasting its own radar signal.

Conventional active radar transmits radio waves and measures their reflections to locate objects. But broadcasting like this is the equivalent of using a powerful searchlight to see in the dark, making the radar station itself highly visible to anyone monitoring the same radio frequencies.

In a recent development, passive radar is not new, but BAE says its use of commercial off-the-shelf equipment brings the cost down to as little as a tenth that of comparable active systems. The equipment is compact enough to deploy from an SUV.

BAE indicates it can track targets ranging from small drones to larger aircraft and provides a clear 3D air picture with data such as target speed, heading, range and altitude. This could make it suitable for law enforcement agencies and for guarding critical national infrastructure, as well as military users.

BAE pitches the system for sites such as airports, where avoiding interference with existing equipment matters. Because it doesn't transmit its own radar signal, passive radar avoids adding another broadcast to the mix.

Sources indicate that "While people are sat at home watching TV, our fresh radar technology can use transmissions from those TV and radio broadcasts without disturbance to keep crucial infrastructure such as power stations and air force bases safe from drone attacks. It also provides a boost for armed forces, allowing a soldier to monitor the battlefield undetected," says BAE's product manager for Counter-Uncrewed Systems (CUxS) Chris Shepherd.

The system will undergo live trials throughout 2027 with potential law enforcement, defense, and critical infrastructure customers, BAE says.

Industry observers note that elsewhere at BAE Systems, the news is less rosy: The Financial Times reports that it plans to shed more than 1,000 jobs at its head office and air division in the UK. The manufacturer says the cuts will help it become more agile and meet government demands for "greater speed and efficiency" in delivering critical defense products. ®.

The financing outlined at Oracle Investor Day, including vendor financing, is in place. Oracle called any further private discussions with vendors “additional options,” said delivery of the OpenAI contract does not depend on them, and preemptively characterized contrary media reports as incorrect.

The stated purpose was to build additional Oracle Cloud Infrastructure capacity for contracted demand from its largest customers, including OpenAI. Oracle planned to raise approximately half through equity-linked and common equity issuances and the other half through a single, one-time issuance of investment-grade senior unsecured bonds early in 2026.

Sources indicate that the equity portion was expected to include an initial issuance of mandatory convertible preferred securities and the at-the-market program. Oracle said in February that it did not expect to issue additional bonds during calendar 2026 beyond the planned transaction.

In a recent development, baseten released bison-1 and groundhog-1 on November 20, 2026, two open-weight models post-trained from Google’s Gemma 4 to return calibrated probabilities for predefined decisions. Artificial Analysis scored bison-1 at 76 on Decision Index v2.1, placing it first among 19 evaluated decision models.

It has been revealed that both are available through Baseten Model APIs and as weights on Hugging Face. They accept text and images and support 131,072 tokens; Baseten claims that is eight times the 16K context of its previous mammoth-1, elephant-1 and joey-1 APIs. A request can bundle one state and any number of yes/no, named-choice or ordered-score questions into one shared-prefix prefill, without generating text.

Recent findings suggest that bison-1 is a dense 31B-parameter model post-trained from Gemma 4 31B. Groundhog-1 is a 26B mixture-of-experts model based on Gemma 4 26B-A4B, with about 4B active parameters per token. Baseten prices them at $0.10 and $0.035 per million tokens, respectively, matching mammoth-1 and elephant-1.

Both use the same API as Baseten’s earlier decision models, and requests above the trained length limits are rejected rather than truncated. Google’s Gemma 4 base models carry Apache License 2.0 terms; Baseten’s modifications are released under the MIT License, with use subject to both licenses.

Recent findings suggest that the Artificial Analysis Decision Index v2.1 combines six evaluations conducted independently by Artificial Analysis. AA-Paperclip, covering decisions and extraction across 1,500 resumes, receipts, invoices and research papers, carries 30% of the weight. The When2Call tool-calling evaluation carries 10%, while tests of workplace judgement, knowledge and hallucination, reasoning and decision invariance each carry 15%.

Its Decision Score subtracts a Brier calibration penalty from accuracy. The underlying probabilities also support confidence thresholds that answer some cases and route others elsewhere, making calibration relevant to how a decision system is deployed.

According to recent reports, artificial Analysis’s November 19, 2026 results place d1.2-ultra second at 75 and mammoth-1 at 71, while bison-1’s 0.14 Brier score is the index’s lowest, against 0.15 for d1.2-ultra. The Brier measure calculates the mean squared gap between the probability assigned to the chosen answer and whether that answer is correct. Lower values indicate confidence that more closely matches actual outcomes.

Sources indicate that the bison-1 model card reports first-place results on When2Call, EvalSafe-O*NET-AA, HLE-MultiChoice v1.1 and AA-Symmetry v1.1, plus second place on AA-Paperclip. Its 60 on AA-Omniscience-Decision v1.1 ranked 11th, so the aggregate lead includes substantial variation across components rather than uniform dominance.

Groundhog-1’s model card states that it has not yet received an Artificial Analysis Decision Index score.

Both models were trained on 6.71 million decision examples spanning core decision skills, safety and abstention, judging and expert domains, documents and long-context tasks, including public benchmark sets. The objective combines cross-entropy with a Brier calibration term and includes a trained I don't know option. About one example in seven carries a probability target instead of a single right answer.

In a recent development, baseten attributes a significant calibration gain to expanding these soft-label targets alongside the Gemma base. Training used 192 B200 GPUs for bison-1 and 128 for groundhog-1.

Industry observers note that in Baseten’s own long-context runs at 128K tokens, bison-1 scored 84.8 on LongMemEval M and 87.1 on LongMemEval S, while groundhog-1 scored 77.4 and 79.3, respectively. These manufacturer-run tests address long-context performance separately from Artificial Analysis’s broader six-part index.

Sources indicate that the release extends long-context, multimodal decision making across both of Base Labs’ established price tiers. Groundhog-1’s independent index result remains the open question for judging whether its mixture-of-experts design delivers the mammoth-1-level performance Baseten expects.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, custom kernels are the backbone of high-performance deep learning, enabling GPU operations tailored precisely to your workload; whether that’s image processing, tensor transformations, or other compute-heavy tasks. But compiling these kernels for the right architectures, wiring all the build flags, and integrating them cleanly into PyTorch extensions can quickly become a mess of CMake/Nix, compiler errors, and ABI problems, which is not fun. Hugging Face’s kernels library makes it easy to build (with kernel-builder) and share these kernels with the kernels-community, with support for multiple GPU and accelerator backends, including CUDA, ROCm, Metal, and XPU. This ensures your kernels are fast, portable, and seamlessly integrated with PyTorch.

In this guide, we focus exclusively on ROCm-compatible kernels and show how to build, test, and share them using kernels. You’ll learn how to create kernels that run efficiently on AMD GPUs, along with best practices for reproducibility, packaging, and deployment.

This ROCm-specific walkthrough is a streamlined version of the original kernel-builder guide. If you’re looking for the broader CUDA-focused version, you can find it here: A Guide to Building and Scaling Production-Ready CUDA Kernels.

We will use the GEMM kernel from RadeonFlow_Kernels as an example. If you want to go straight to the guide, click here.

This section was written by the RadeonFlow GEMM kernel authors to introduce the kernel.Authors: ColorsWind, Zesen Liu, and Andy.

The RadeonFlow GEMM kernel is a high-performance, FP8 block-wise matrix multiplication implementation optimized for the AMD Instinct MI300X GPU. GEMM (General Matrix Multiplication) is the core building block behind most deep learning workloads: given two matrices A and B, you compute their product C = A × B. Here it’s implemented in FP8, a low-precision floating-point format that trades a bit of accuracy for much higher throughput and lower memory bandwidth. This kernel was developed for the AMD Developer Challenge 2025, it was awarded the 🏆 Grand Prize in June 2025, recognizing its excellence in performance and innovation on AMD hardware.

Sources indicate that the kernel operates on quantized inputs using the e4m3fnuz floating-point format and applies per-block scaling to preserve accuracy during low-precision computation. The e4m3fnuz format is an FP8 variant with 4 exponent bits and 3 mantissa bits, designed to be efficient for neural network workloads. Because FP8 has a much smaller dynamic range than FP16/FP32, we apply per-block scaling factors (a_scale and b_scale) so that each block of values is rescaled into a numerically “comfortable” range before and after computation, which helps preserve accuracy despite the low precision. It takes the following arguments:.

where a and b are the input matrices, a_scale and b_scale are the scaling factors for a and b respectively, and c is the output matrix:.

The kernel is precompiled for specific matrix shapes and assumes a transposed memory layout (as required by the competition). To support additional shapes or alternative memory layouts, you must modify the kernel launcher.

So now that we have a high-performance ROCm kernel, the natural question is: how do we integrate it into a real PyTorch workflow and share it with others? That’s exactly what we’ll cover next, using kernels to structure, build, and publish the ROCm kernel.

In a recent development, this is a fairly technical guide, but you can still follow it step by step without understanding every detail and everything will work fine. If you’re curious, you can always come back later to dig deeper into the concepts.

The shared encoder gives the upgrade relevance beyond FSD, extending into Tesla’s robotaxi and Optimus programs.

For driver monitoring, Tesla reports greater availability of vision-based attention monitoring when drivers wear hats or sunglasses, with reduced strictness in higher-speed driver profiles.   • Nov 22, 2026 2 min read.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Google Announces Agent Compute Engine for Secure AI Agent Execution.

Nov 22, 2026 2 min read.

Google recently announced Agent Compute Engine, a managed service that runs AI agents in isolated microVMs, with checkpointing capabilities to suspend and resume execution environments. The design keeps credentials, API keys, and OAuth refresh tokens outside the agent sandbox, using an external Agent Gateway to authenticate requests and inject the required secrets.

Google designed Agent Compute Engine to address three requirements at global scale: keeping sandboxes free of exploitable credentials, even when agents make mistakes; minimizing the cost and latency of resuming idle agents; and preserving persistent workspaces across sessions and operating system updates. The infrastructure team writes:.

Agent Compute Engine achieves this by using copy-on-write memory sharing to run multiple agents on a single operating system template, and pausing idle microVMs via fast checkpoint and restore.

In the deep dive "Inside Agent Compute Engine," Ramanathan Venkatapathy and Rohit Jnagal, distinguished engineers at Google, describe the service’s architecture, covering microVM isolation, credential management, agent identity, storage, and scheduling at scale. They explain the strict separation between the agent harness and sandbox:.

The orchestration harness (the brain) runs completely outside the execution sandbox (the hands), helping ensure that untrusted guest environments only execute explicit commands dispatched by the harness and stream output back. This boundary establishes a deterministic audit trail correlating every harness-initiated tool call with expected compute activity inside the sandbox.

The architecture supports four main workload categories: interactive consumer and enterprise agents that execute code, browse the web, and perform actions; persistent Linux workspaces for autonomous software engineering; large-scale parallel environments for model evaluation and reinforcement learning; and lightweight, sandboxed execution environments for dynamic logic in Google services.

Venkatapathy and Jnagal also describe how the cloud provider uses the platform internally for Gemini, Gemini for Business, the agentic development platform Antigravity, and model evaluation workloads.

Separately, Google offers Agent Substrate, an open-source, Kubernetes-native runtime for running AI agents in isolated environments. Agent Substrate manages sandbox lifecycles independently of the underlying compute infrastructure, allowing idle agents to be suspended while preserving their state and resuming execution on available workers when needed.

In the article "Google's Agent Compute Engine: A MicroVM Sandbox With No Credentials Inside, and What Google Has Not Shipped Yet," Harel Asaf, AI specialist at Elementor, examines the security architecture, the separation of credentials from agent execution environments, and the gaps between Google's announcement and what is presently available. Asaf warns:.

It has been revealed that the deep dive gives no boot time, price or density figure for Agent Compute Engine itself. It indicates developers will control each environment's image, identity, network access and lifecycle, while Google manages the fleet, and that the service is targeted for preview in the coming months. The numbers in the announcement belong to Agent Substrate.

Industry observers note that google is not the only provider offering managed, isolated execution environments for AI agents, with AWS and Azure providing similar capabilities through Bedrock AgentCore and Foundry Agent Service. However, Google’s approach keeps credentials outside agent sandboxes and injects them through an external gateway.

Google also expanded its agent governance capabilities with centralized identity and policy enforcement: the governance stack includes Agent Gateway for traffic control and policy enforcement, Agent Registry for tracking approved agents and tools, SPIFFE-based Agent Identity for authentication and auditing, and OpenTelemetry-compatible observability for monitoring model calls and tool invocations.

Agent Compute Engine is not yet available, and pricing has not been revealed. The cloud provider is targeting a preview in the coming months. While Agent Substrate is portable across Kubernetes environments, Agent Compute Engine itself is limited to Google Cloud.

Apriel-H1: The Surprising Key to Distilling Efficient Reasoning Models

📅 19 Nov 2025 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1575 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that we converted our 15B reasoning model to a Mamba hybrid achieving 2.1x throughput with minimal quality loss.
  • When MiniMax published their M2 post-mortem in October explaining why they abandoned efficient attention at 230B scale, the narrative briefly became "efficient attention is dead." Within days, Kimi Linear proved otherwise.
  • Our constraint was simple: we had a strong 15B reasoning model and needed to make it efficient without starting over.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that we converted our 15B reasoning model to a Mamba hybrid achieving 2.1x throughput with minimal quality loss. The key? A non-obvious insight about what data to distill on, and why intuition fails here.

When MiniMax published their M2 post-mortem in October explaining why they abandoned efficient attention at 230B scale, the narrative briefly became "efficient attention is dead." Within days, Kimi Linear proved otherwise. The real lesson: it depends on your constraints.

Our constraint was simple: we had a strong 15B reasoning model and needed to make it efficient without starting over. No infinite compute for 20T-token pretraining. No luxury of architectural co-design from day one. Just a practical question: can you retrofit efficiency into an existing model through distillation?

Spoilers: yes, but only if you ignore your intuition about what data to use.

According to recent reports, the Apriel-H1 family: seven checkpoints spanning 25-40 Mamba layers (out of 50 total), showing the complete efficiency-quality frontier. Our flagship Apriel-H1-15b-Thinker-SFT achieves 2.1x throughput with minimal quality loss: MATH500 and MTBench improve a few points (0.90 → 0.92 and 8.30 → 8.58, respectively), while GSM8k (0.97 → 0.95), GPQA (0.59 → 0.55), and AIME24 (0.70 → 0.65) regress slightly. Total training: 76.8B tokens.

It has been revealed that apriel-H1-15b-Thinker-SFT (green) vs full-attention teacher (blue). Reasoning quality stays nearly flat across benchmarks while throughput increases 1.89-2.09x depending on context length.

The full details are in our Apriel-H1 paper. Here, we focus on the key insight that made it work.

Here's what we initially thought would work: just distill on pretraining data and round it out with some SFT.

The reasoning seemed solid. We're inserting completely new Mamba layers that have never seen data. These linear SSMs need to learn general-purpose token mixing from scratch. How can they become effective mixers unless they get exposure to the same broad distribution the original attention layers saw?

So we tried it. Then we tried mixing pretraining and SFT data. It didn't work. The distilled hybrids lost reasoning quality, sometimes dramatically.

What actually worked: high-quality reasoning traces from the teacher's SFT dataset.

Sources indicate that distilling a reasoning model isn't about transferring general next-token prediction. The base model already has that, and we started from a strong 15B foundation. What we're preserving is specific and fragile: the teacher's multi-step reasoning patterns.

Those patterns emerge from intricate attention mechanisms. Retrieval heads pulling context from thousands of tokens back. Induction heads recognizing and continuing logical chains. Long-range dependencies connecting premises to conclusions many steps later. When you replace attention wholesale with Mamba's linear recurrence, these computational mechanisms are disrupted. The hybrid must discover new paths to the same reasoning outcomes.

That discovery requires explicit examples where reasoning structure is visible and correct:.

Pretraining data, on the other hand, is too noisy and too diffuse. The reasoning signal gets lost. You need concentrated examples of the specific capability you're trying to preserve.

Once we understood the data choice, our distillation method became clear too. We used reverse KL divergence (temperature 1) rather than forward KL. Reverse won consistently. Why? We're training on problems where the teacher has high confidence and clear structure. Reverse KL's mode-seeking behavior encourages the student to commit to those high-confidence predictions. When your teacher is confident and correct, you want your student to be confident too.

This insight is the key to the whole approach: match your distillation data to the capability you're preserving, not the capability you're building.

You can't just swap 40 attention layers for Mamba and hope. We learned this the hard way, and eventually developed a staged distillation procedure to get there reliably.

Stage 1: Identify least-vital layers. We used a Leave-One-Out (LOO) analysis on MMLU: remove each layer, replace with identity, then measure the drop. Sort by importance, replace the bottom 25 with Mamba-in-Llama (MIL) initialized mixers. Distill end-to-end. This worked for our H-25 checkpoint.

In a recent development, stage 2: Progressive conversion beyond 25 layers. LOO broke down past 25 layers because layers unimportant in isolation became critical in combination. To address this, we developed a dynamic heuristic we call MIL-Mamba-Replacement (MMR). For each remaining attention layer, we initialize a Mamba mixer with MIL, run 100 training steps, and record the distillation loss. Layers converging to lower loss are "easier" to replace. This captures training dynamics rather than static importance.

In a recent development, we progressed incrementally: 25 → 27 → 30 → 34 → 37 → 40 Mamba layers, grouping replacements by MMR scores. Each checkpoint distills from the previous.

Recent findings suggest that stage 3: End-to-end training on SFT data. After reaching the target Mamba layer count, we did a final SFT pass until reasoning performance stabilized. After 55.9B distillation tokens and 20.9B SFT tokens, this produced our final Apriel-H1-15b-Thinker-SFT model.

The complete efficiency frontier. Each checkpoint demonstrates cumulative training tokens. Our flagship H-30-SFT (released as Apriel-H1-15b-Thinker-SFT) used 76.8B total for 2.1x throughput at 0.76 average score. The aggressively converted H-40 variant used 136.5B tokens for 3.4x throughput. For reference: NVIDIA's Nemotron-Nano-9B-v2 achieves 4.6x at 0.77 score but required training from scratch with orders of magnitude more compute.

We built all this on Fast-LLM, our open-source training framework. The core architectural principle: large language model transformers should be modular. Attention and Mamba are different implementations of the same "mixing" interface, and can be swapped freely.

Here's a hybrid architecture in Fast-LLM's config format:.

Industry observers note that the pattern field specifies layer order. For Apriel-H1-15b-Thinker-SFT: 30 mamba_block, 20 attention_block, placed by importance. That's it.

Distillation is configuration too:.

Fast-LLM handles gradient accumulation, distributed training, tensor parallelism, checkpointing, everything you need for large-scale experimentation. It's open source, and licensed under Apache 2.0. You can reproduce this work because we designed the infrastructure to make it reproducible.

Recent findings suggest that why release all checkpoints? Because optimal depends on your constraints. H-30 offers the best balance. H-40 maximizes throughput for latency-critical workloads. The intermediate checkpoints let you choose your exact trade-off.

Recent findings suggest that why do you get different speedups at different context lengths? Mamba's linear complexity advantage grows with sequence length, and attention degrades quadratically.

Industry observers note that why did you only try Mamba? We used Mamba-1 for three reasons: it has a proven distillation track record, has shown strong empirical performance, and was simple to implement in our framework. It let us focus on the data question first.

Recent findings suggest that what were the Mamba hyperparameters? State size 16, DT rank 16, inner dimension 4096. For our GQA setup in Apriel we expanded B (input projection) and x (state) to match total attention heads following M1.

Recent findings suggest that why didn't you try more advanced conversion methods? We used Mamba-in-Llama initialization and knowledge distillation rather than MOHAWK's multi-stage procedure because the latter didn't show significant advantages in preliminary experiments.

Sources indicate that why did you only SFT the H-30 model? We only applied SFT to H-30 to validate that distilled hybrids can be improved through standard post-training. The other checkpoints are pure distillation but can be fine-tuned similarly.

It has been revealed that why didn't you explore RL? This was a scoping decision to isolate the distillation question: can you transfer reasoning via knowledge distillation alone? Answer: yes. But RL should close remaining quality gaps further. We are exploring RL for future iterations.

Did you really show that Apriel-H1 matches full-attention reasoning at similar compute budgets? We didn't do an apples-to-apples comparison between full-attention Apriel and a hybrid trained identically from pretraining forward. That would require repeating all mid-training and post-training of the teacher with the Apriel-H1 architecture, which was beyond our compute budget. What we can claim though is that retrofitting efficiency via distillation is practical and effective, and that the resulting hybrids can be fine-tuned to match or exceed the teacher's reasoning quality.

Sources indicate that we've implemented Apriel-H1 in Hugging Face Transformers and vLLM. Transformers integration is straightforward. We ship a newly introduced model class with interchangeable attention and Mamba layers. vLLM integration uses their recent Mamba cache operations for continuous batching, prefix caching, and chunked prefill. The vLLM plugin is ready. We are at the moment waiting for final legal approval to open-source it.

According to recent reports, honest assessment: Deploying hybrids today means rough edges. The tooling is maturing fast but isn't turnkey. You will write custom code, validate numerical behavior carefully, and work around framework limitations. For teams that can absorb that cost, throughput gains are worth it. For those that can't, waiting might be the right call.

Most teams don't have infinite compute for 20T-token pretraining. If you've invested in a strong base model and need efficiency gains, this work shows a practical path: distill into hybrids using high-quality task-specific data that matches the capability you're preserving.

Industry observers note that the surprising finding, use reasoning data to distill reasoning, seems obvious in retrospect but contradicts initial intuition. We validated it, explained why it works, and built the infrastructure to make it reproducible.

Models: Apriel-H1 Collection on HuggingFaceTraining framework: Fast-LLM on GitHubTeacher model: Apriel-Nemotron-15B-ThinkerPaper: Apriel-H1: Towards Efficient Enterprise Reasoning Models.

Sources indicate that found something broken? File an glitch. Discovered a better layer placement heuristic? Tell us. Built something interesting on Apriel-H1? We'd love to see it.

Gliver completes the Guix desktop

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1546 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dustycloud

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Christine Lemmer-Webber on Sun 22 November 2026.
  • Industry observers note that there's a bit of irony in the title.
  • Notably, that release will be 0.0.5.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Christine Lemmer-Webber on Sun 22 November 2026.

Industry observers note that there's a bit of irony in the title. At the time of writing, Gliver, a Guile based window manager for Wayland in the style of StumpWM and Emacs, isn't yet in Guix. There is, however, an open PR to add Gliver to Guix. However, what that patch is really waiting on is an upcoming release of Gliver which will solve many bugs.

Notably, that release will be 0.0.5. If that sounds early, Gliver still is early. There are bugs, and you will probably have to file concerns for some that you discover. There are also some noticeable missing features. But it doesn't matter. Gliver is everything I want from a desktop experience, and I suspect for many of the kinds of people who read my blog, it will be for them as well.

It has been revealed that gliver might not be for everyone. But if the following appeals to you: a live-hackable, written in Guile Scheme, tiling window manager which looks good, feels good, and whose codebase is understandable and, indeed, encourages you to understand and explore it, Gliver is for you.

I think Anna Liberty's Towards Understandable Software is a must-read. Call it a counter-vision to the vibe bobsled. Anna lays out that software should be more understandable, not less, and easy to participate in even for people with no programming background. While Gliver doesn't itself try all the approaches Anna lays out, it is an understandable codebase.

Furthermore, Gliver is participatory. Gliver invites you to learn its internals and explore it. By default, Gliver's describe-key functionality opens a window where you can type the command you are thinking of, and it will show you what key it is bound to... but you can also type in a key sequence, and it'll show you what command that runs.

According to recent reports, more than that, by default Gliver opens a unix domain socket in ~/.local/state/gliver/repl.sock. You can connect to this, say with Geiser. You are live! You know that command you just looked up with the above describe-key interface? Why not try running it at the REPL! Hey, how does it work? Well Geiser already has a feature for that; by default typing M-. (geiser-edit-symbol-at-point) will jump you right to the definition, and you can explore how that code works! You can run commands manually at the REPL, you can inspect the state of the system, you can hack away, you can take the useful things you have learned and add them to your init.scm file so that the next time Gliver starts things are more the way you want them than last time. But of course there's no need to wait, this is a lisp style system! You can eval those changes and apply them immediately and carry on your way.

It has been revealed that maybe this all sounds pretty technical, and even technically elite. And I think Gliver is probably not very accessible to non-scheme-hackers. But on the other hand, it could help you become a Scheme hacker.

When I started using Emacs, I was not a programmer. By extending Emacs, I became a programmer. (My background is not in CS; I was an interdisciplinary humanities student.) Emacs invites you to explore how it works by customizing it. My entire career would not have likely happened if Emacs did not welcome me into this process.

Recent findings suggest that gliver takes the same approach. But instead of Emacs Lisp, which is a hackable but honestly not really great lisp, it uses Guile Scheme, which is lovely. And notably, this is the same language as Guix.

There is more I want to say on this, and I will in a future article. In many ways I think Blender is also an interesting example of reflective software in action, and actually does expose some of the ideas such as visual programming for non-programmers in a way that Emacs and Gliver don't, with great success too. But that's to discuss later.

It has been revealed that but as for the choice to switch. I have gotten tired of using systems that feel like they know better than I do. I have spent most of my days using GNOME, but without getting too much into it, I have been burnt way too many times by a paternalistic attitude which seems at the center of its design philosophy. When I did the latest upgrade and found out that custom application launcher shortcuts did not work anymore, and I could not figure out for the life of me why, I decided I didn't actually care to try to solve the problem this time. I was going to try something else.

Which is when I re-discovered Gliver. Thanks to ebeem for working on Gliver and jfred for having been an earlier adopter than I was and who helped me with some messy this-isnt-yet-packaged trickiness.

I suppose I've already said most of it, but a few more details. One interesting aspect of Gliver is that it uses River, which is a Wayland compositor which is designed as a framework for building window managers on top of. Building small window managers had become a lot harder to do with the move from X11 to Wayland; River provides a common foundation that makes it much more possible.

Recent findings suggest that gliver allegedly supports different tiling modes, but I don't use them, I just use manual tiling. I like splitting up my screens the way I like them. I know I want this thing here and that thing there. Gliver shines at this kind of manual flow. It also has multiple "tabbed" windows stacked in each pane of the frames (in Gliver, each of those panes is called a "container"). You can move around what workspace and container a window "belongs to" with keybindings. Personally I bound -x to be a keymapping with sub-bindings for splitting things up with the same equivalent keys as they are in emacs, since those mappings are burned into my brain.

It has been revealed that the default theme is very nice. You can customize its colors but black and purple is exactly my jam already.

In a recent development, there are some rough edges. I have filed a number of issues for the things I've encountered. But one of the most noticeable is that there are several commands you might find for launching shell commands or creating new workspaces where you would expect to be prompted. For example, here's one of Gliver's commands for running a shell command:.

According to recent reports, nice, these look like good commands, let's bind them to keys in our config! But oh wait, nothing happens! That's strange, they work at the REPL, why don't they work when bound to a key?

The simple answer is that #:interactive (string) part you see above, which indicates that Gliver's UI should be asking you for a prompt and letting you type in something, simply isn't implemented yet! So when I say there are some missing features, there really are some missing features.

But this all may be changing very rapidly. ebeem is working on a refactor of the GUI system to be more of a functional reactive programming type system, inspired by Flutter. When that lands, I expect a number of bugs to be fixed, and a number of missing features like the above to land.

This does lead to the funny situation that to create a fresh workspace, I have to do it at the REPL! That's okay. It'll be fixed, and for now, it's a nice reminder that running things at the REPL is something I can absolutely do at any time with Gliver, which I appreciate.

Speaking of the GUI, what GUI toolkit is it using, you may wonder? The answer is: it kind of has its own thing! Gliver has FFI bindings to Cairo for its vector graphics and Pango for fonts. That's it! It seems to be a good enough foundation for the rest it is using and doing.

Recent findings suggest that now, how am I running Gliver at all when it isn't in Guix? The funny thing is that for now, I am running out of a git checkout of Gliver. I start up and sacrifice the not-so-proverbial Cow window manager and replace it live with Gliver in a terminal like so:.

Which is basically the trick in the Gliver README, just starting with a cow sacrifice first. Pretty ugly though, it'll be nicer when Gliver is just packaged in Guix.

Gliver is nice. It feels good, it works well. And it's participatory, understandable software. It's also very early. It might not be for everyone, but it has elements of a vision for a future I'd like to see for everyone.

If you like the idea of a scheme'y lisp machine using Guix as your operating system distribution but have found that the desktop experience was missing, well, Gliver is now here! And soon, packaged in a Guix near you.

In a recent development, and, I suspect, once it is... well, we'll be seeing most of the Guix community moving over. It's too exciting and too nice not to!

As cars go digital, US consumers pay an extra $12 billion a year for repairs

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (559 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today's vehicles need software tools to make repairs, and the subscriptions inflate insurance fees.
  • The computerization of cars comes at a price to US consumers, according to the Public Interest Research Group (PIRG), which notes that software fees and other charges faced by mechanics push up garage costs.
  • Industry observers note that an investigation by the non-profit consumer group estimates that car repair costs for Americans have been inflated by $12 billion each year, as vehicles integrate more computerized functions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today's vehicles need software tools to make repairs, and the subscriptions inflate insurance fees.

The computerization of cars comes at a price to US consumers, according to the Public Interest Research Group (PIRG), which notes that software fees and other charges faced by mechanics push up garage costs.

Industry observers note that an investigation by the non-profit consumer group estimates that car repair costs for Americans have been inflated by $12 billion each year, as vehicles integrate more computerized functions. Its report, Closing Shop, is available online.

To find a failed sensor, release an electronic parking brake, or perform diagnostics, a technician has to first connect a laptop or tablet to the vehicle. To so this, the repair shop has to have the right software tools, and that means paying the vehicle manufacturer subscription charges and other fees, in order to get the information they need to complete the job.

If smaller independent repair shops can’t afford all the necessary software or subscriptions, they may be forced to steer customers to authorized dealerships for some fixes – about one in five jobs – and this allows the latter to charge more.

PIRG claims that drivers pay for this through their insurance premiums, even if they never need to get their car fixed, because higher repair costs mean higher insurance claims. It says the price of auto insurance has risen three times as fast as the rest of the US economy since 2012.

Sources indicate that even if mechanics do choose to pay for the software, they spend an estimated collective 83 million hours a year buying, downloading, logging in, and waiting. At typical repair rates, that adds up to $12 billion.

A separate report from the PIRG Education Fund claims that a two-tiered repair model now exists, where independent sites conduct repairs with less information, less powerful diagnostic tools, and higher associated costs than the authorized dealerships.

The advocacy group wants to see legislators take this glitch in hand, and has a number of recommendations for them. One is to stop manufacturers from locking out independent mechanics from simple repair jobs like changing brake pads, and require them to support a standard protocol for authenticating independent diagnostic tools.

Industry observers note that another is to give owners control over their vehicle’s data via a standardized platform for accessing telematics repair information, so that the owner can give access to an independent repair shop. Car firms can use the vehicle data to tell owners that a repair is needed and to take it to an approved repair shop, without even disclosing what the problem is.

According to recent reports, DIY repairers should be able to get everything they need to fix their own cars. Service information and basic diagnostic software should be free, and PIRG also wants a cap on the license fees manufacturers charge for their official software tools.

“We’ve allowed car manufacturers to build a toll road between the mechanic and the repair,” claims Nathan Proctor, leader of PIRG’s Right to Repair campaign and co-author on the report.

“We have a plethora of tolls on the road – subscriptions you need for manuals, diagnostic tools, secure access and more. Not only are all these tolls expensive, they also create traffic jams, slowing down the whole process, which adds to the costs for consumers.”  ®.
