📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The robot completes the pick. The audience applauds. What the short video cannot show is the worker who reset the tray, the remote operator who rescued an earlier attempt or the hours the machine spent waiting for help. A demonstration can be entirely real and still leave the business question unanswered.

For robotics in 2027, the revealing unit will be a stretch of ordinary operation: changing objects, imperfect lighting, interrupted connectivity and nobody standing conveniently beside the cell to make the next attempt work.

The International Federation of Robotics' 2026 report documents a large, established industrial robot base. Meanwhile, Gemini Robotics 2 represents a newer research direction toward broader embodied capability. Those are different kinds of evidence. The following forecasts concern the difficult passage from flexible demonstrations to dependable operations.

It has been revealed that A robot that asks for help every few minutes can move labor around without removing much of it. In 2027, more suppliers and operators will make that burden visible through interventions per task or operating hour. Buyers will be able to ask a better question than whether the machine succeeded: how much attention did success consume?

Industry observers note that success rate alone can hide expensive labor. If a robot completes a task after an operator rearranges the objects, the work may still be useful, but the support belongs in the economic calculation. The same applies to remote assistance, resets and recovery after a dropped object.

In a recent development, deepMind's responsible robotics material illustrates why evaluation has to consider behavior beyond a task-completion score. My prediction is that commercial pressure will make intervention reporting more visible, although definitions will remain inconsistent. A warehouse customer can tolerate assistance if its cost is known; it cannot price an undisclosed dependency.

Industry observers note that the demanding test is sustained operation over varied shifts, rather than many repetitions in an unchanged scene. Reporting must also distinguish a safety stop from a routine request for help. Reducing all stops indiscriminately would be a poor objective: an appropriate stop can prevent damage while revealing a limit the deployment needs to address.

Sources indicate that look for denominators, shift lengths, task boundaries and explicit treatment of remote assistance. An intervention metric that excludes resets or workspace preparation will be less informative. Repeated results at customer sites would strengthen the prediction more than another laboratory highlight reel.

According to recent reports, estimate labor per completed unit, including supervision and recovery. Pilot agreements should specify what counts as assistance and who records it. A somewhat slower robot may produce better economics if it runs predictably and requires less skilled attention when something goes wrong.

Industry observers note that A network outage should not turn a recoverable grasp into a helpless machine. In 2027, commercial pilots will demonstrate bounded recovery using learned models on the robot itself. The interesting capability will be modest and practical: recognizing a failed attempt, choosing an allowed response and knowing when another attempt would make matters worse.

Robots already use local control for timing-critical motion. The new question is how much adaptable perception and task reasoning can remain available when a remote service is slow or unreachable. A machine should not need a network round trip to decide that an attempted grasp has failed and that it should stop safely.

According to recent reports, gemini Robotics On-Device and its On-Device 2 model card provide current examples of work toward local embodied intelligence. They do not demonstrate unrestricted competence in every customer environment. Hardware memory, power and heat still constrain the size and frequency of inference.

It has been revealed that I expect a layered architecture: deterministic safety controls, local perception and bounded recovery, with remote resources available for slower planning or fleet learning. This preserves useful behavior during disconnection without pretending that a small model can resolve every unexpected situation. Some failures should end in a request for help rather than a more elaborate autonomous attempt.

Sources indicate that look for actual disconnection tests, the tasks attempted offline, and what the machine refuses to do. Latency measurements should include sensing and execution. A cloud-connected demonstration marketed as edge autonomy would not establish the forecast.

Recent findings suggest that ask suppliers to demonstrate the degraded mode at your site. Define which operations may continue, which must pause, and how the robot reconciles state after reconnecting. The value of local inference includes predictable availability, not merely avoiding cloud inference charges.

In a recent development, the route to a useful generalist may begin with a second job in the same room. I expect deployments to expand into adjacent tasks in 2027, with performance reported separately. Reusing the environment, tools and integration can make flexibility valuable long before one machine can take over the full variety of a person's shift.

General-purpose models make transfer more plausible, but a factory is not a single task. Changing the tool, container or object material can change contact dynamics and sensing requirements. Reusing a learned representation helps only if the rest of the system can support the latest work.

The progression from Gemini Robotics 1.5 to Robotics 2 shows how rapidly the research capabilities are moving. Commercial transfer will still depend on tooling, fixtures, task data and integration with existing processes. My forecast is deliberately about adjacent tasks in a familiar environment, where those costs can be shared.

It has been revealed that this is a more credible route to utilization than expecting one machine to perform an entire worker's varied responsibilities. It also gives operators a way to compare generalization with ordinary task-specific engineering. If the second task needs a complete redevelopment, the supposed flexibility has not yet created much operational advantage.

Look for adaptation time, latest demonstrations required, tooling changes and performance on both tasks after the expansion. A second promotional video without operating results would be weak evidence. Maintaining the original task's reliability will matter as much as adding the new capability.

Choose pilots with a clear second use case nearby. Sharing an operating environment can improve utilization without creating an unmanageable support burden. Negotiate adaptation work and acceptance criteria early, so the promised flexibility is reflected in delivery obligations and price.

Industry observers note that A robot can recognize a gauge without reading it correctly, and read it without understanding what the value permits. In 2027, evaluations will connect these intermediate judgments to completed physical tasks. That will expose a richer question than object recognition: does the machine understand enough of the current state to take the next appropriate action?

Recognizing a valve is different from reading its position; recognizing a gauge is different from understanding whether the current reading permits the next action. These intermediate judgments can determine whether an otherwise capable manipulation policy behaves appropriately.

Industry observers note that gemini Robotics-ER 1.6 highlights embodied reasoning and instrument interpretation as active research areas. The crucial next step is connecting those outputs to a measured operational consequence. A benchmark of photographs alone cannot establish reliable behavior under changing lighting, vibration, partial visibility and sensor disagreement.

Some applications will still need dedicated sensors because a visual estimate is insufficient. Progress in visual reasoning should make that engineering choice more informed, rather than eliminate it by assumption.

It has been revealed that look for ambiguous readings, unusual viewpoints and explicit abstention when evidence is insufficient. A useful evaluation will distinguish perception failures from planning and execution failures. Scores on easy images without a downstream task would offer less support.

According to recent reports, specify the physical measurements required by the process and their acceptable error. Use calibrated instrumentation where the consequence warrants it. A robot's fluent account of what it sees should be checked against the measurements needed to run the operation safely and consistently.

The next persuasive robotics story may contain fewer spectacular movements and a much longer operating record. A machine that works predictably, recovers sensibly and asks for help at the right moment can be enormously valuable. The shift begins when buyers can see the labor surrounding the robot as clearly as the robot itself.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, LLMs have become essential tools for building software.
  • Developers building AI-powered apps typically take a hybrid approach, adopting some combination of:.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, LLMs have become essential tools for building software. But for Apple developers, integrating them remains unnecessarily painful.

Developers building AI-powered apps typically take a hybrid approach, adopting some combination of:.

In a recent development, each comes with different APIs, different requirements, different integration patterns. It's a lot, and it adds up quickly. When I interviewed developers about building AI-powered apps, friction with model integration came up immediately. One developer put it bluntly:.

It has been revealed that I thought I'd rapidly use the demo for a test and maybe a quick and dirty build but instead wasted so much time. Drove me nuts.

The cost to experiment is high, which discourages developers from discovering that local, open-source models might actually work great for their use case.

Today we're announcing AnyLanguageModel, a Swift package that provides a drop-in replacement for Apple's Foundation Models framework with support for multiple model providers. Our goal is to reduce the friction of working with LLMs on Apple platforms and make it easier to adopt open-source models that run locally.

The core idea is simple: Swap your import statement, keep the same API.

Here's what that looks like in practice. Start with Apple's built-in model:.

Now try an open-source model running locally via MLX:.

AnyLanguageModel supports a range of providers:.

Sources indicate that the focus is on local models that you can download from the Hugging Face Hub. Cloud providers are included to lower the barrier to getting started and to provide a migration path. Make it work, then make it right.

When designing AnyLanguageModel, we faced a choice: create a upcoming abstraction that tries to capture everything, or build on an existing API. We chose the latter, using Apple's Foundation Models framework as the template.

This might seem counterintuitive. Why tie ourselves to Apple's choices? A few reasons:.

Sources indicate that foundation Models is genuinely well-designed. It leverages Swift features like macros for an ergonomic developer experience, and its abstractions around sessions, tools, and generation map well to how LLMs actually work.

It has been revealed that it's intentionally limited. Foundation Models represents something like a lowest common denominator for language model capabilities. Rather than seeing this as a weakness, we treat it as a stable foundation (hyuk hyuk). Every Swift developer targeting Apple platforms will encounter this API, so building on it directly means less conceptual overhead.

It keeps us grounded. Each additional layer of abstraction takes you further from the problem you're actually solving. Abstractions are powerful, but stack too many and they become a problem in themselves.

The result is that switching between providers requires minimal code changes, and the core abstractions remain clean and predictable.

One challenge with multi-backend libraries is dependency bloat. If you only want to run MLX models, you shouldn't have to pull in llama.cpp and all its dependencies.

Sources indicate that anyLanguageModel uses Swift 6.1 package traits to solve this. You opt in to only the backends you need:.

Sources indicate that available traits include CoreML, MLX, and Llama (for llama.cpp / llama.swift). By default, no heavy dependencies are included. You get the base API plus cloud providers, which only require standard URLSession networking.

For Xcode projects (which don't yet support trait declarations directly), you can create a small internal Swift package that depends on AnyLanguageModel with the traits you need, then add that package as a local dependency. The README has detailed instructions.

Vision-language models are incredibly capable and widely used. They can describe images, extract text from screenshots, analyze charts, and answer questions about visual content. Unfortunately, Apple's Foundation Models framework doesn't presently support sending images with prompts.

According to recent reports, building on an existing API means accepting its constraints. Apple will likely add image support in a future release (iOS 27, perhaps?), but vision-language models are too useful to wait for. So we've extended beyond what Foundation Models offers today.

Here's an example sending an image to Claude:.

We're taking a calculated risk here; we might design something that conflicts with Apple's eventual implementation. But that's what deprecation warnings are for. Sometimes you have to write the API for the framework that doesn't exist yet.

To see AnyLanguageModel in action, check out chat-ui-swift, a SwiftUI chat application that demonstrates the library's capabilities.

In a recent development, it's meant as a starting point: Fork it, extend it, swap in different models. See how the pieces fit together and adapt it to your needs.

AnyLanguageModel is right now pre-1.0. The core API is stable, but we're actively working on bringing the full feature set of Foundation Models to all adapters, namely:.

This library is the first step toward something larger. A unified inference API provides the scaffolding needed to build seamless agentic workflows on Apple platforms — applications where models can use tools, access system resources, and accomplish complex tasks. More on that soon. 🤫.

We'd love your help making this better:.

We're excited to see what you build 🦾.

#126369. Falsehoods Programmers Believe About ATProto

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 24m • 📚 Deep Dive (4802 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Reiver ↗ Open Full Page

Falsehoods Programmers Believe About ATProto

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 24 min read (4802 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reiver

⏱️ ~24 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the year 2010, Patrick McKenzie wrote and published the article “Falsehoods Programmers Believe About Names” — a list of reasonable-sounding assumptions about people's names that not only were not true, but also (if assumed) would create bugs and even break software.
  • Every numbered statement below is false.
  • According to recent reports, these are not made up for effect.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the year 2010, Patrick McKenzie wrote and published the article “Falsehoods Programmers Believe About Names” — a list of reasonable-sounding assumptions about people's names that not only were not true, but also (if assumed) would create bugs and even break software. That article started a whole genre of Falsehoods Programmers Believe articles. This article ("Falsehoods Programmers Believe About ATProto") is one of my contributions to that genre.

Every numbered statement below is false. Each one is followed by what is actually true — and where to read more.

According to recent reports, these are not made up for effect. Each one is backed by the specification, or by a live request to real ATProto servers (made in November 2026).

Sources indicate that handles can change. The account's DID is what is permanent — the accounts specification calls it (DIDs) “unique and immutable”.

My handle changed! My handle was first reiver.bsky.social, then became reiver.myatproto.social, and then later became reiver.blacksky.team. You can see that if you dig through the data at plc.directory/did:plc:scewmn2pl3oz36mxme2b6czz/log/audit. (did:plc:scewmn2pl3oz36mxme2b6czz is my DID-PLC DID.).

So, a handle is a good database key for a user.

Use the DID. Store the handle only for display (cosmetic) purposes — and re-check what each DID's handle is from time to time.

Industry observers note that but, you need to normalize the DID before using it. DIDs are URIs, and URI schemes are case-insensitive (RFC 3986) — so DID:plc:scewmn2pl3oz36mxme2b6czz and did:plc:scewmn2pl3oz36mxme2b6czz are the same DID. ATProto requires the normalized (lowercase) form: normalize DIDs when they come from user input, store and compare only the normalized form, and reject non-normalized DIDs that arrive in protocol data.

When a user changes their handle, the first part stays the same — such as reiver.bsky.social → reiver.myatproto.social → reiver.blacksky.team.

A upcoming handle does not have to have anything in common with the old one. joeblow.bsky.social → me.example.com → bbqlover.net → ilikeicecream.com would be fine. Changing a handle just means pointing the account at a different domain — com.atproto.identity.updateHandle takes any valid handle, and only “Verifies handle validity”.

Industry observers note that for example, Bluesky's own account (did:plc:z72i7hdynmk6r22z27h6tvur) started out as bluesky-team.bsky.social, and then became bsky.app. You can see that in its audit log at plc.directory/did:plc:z72i7hdynmk6r22z27h6tvur/log/audit. (Another reason to key users by DID, and not by any part of their handle.).

You can trust a handle you saw five minutes ago.

A handle can change at any moment. The user can switch to a latest handle. The domain's owner can point it at a different DID — or the domain can expire, and be registered by someone else. Or, its DNS record or /.well-known/atproto-did file can just disappear, and the handle stops resolving. The handle specification states “If the handle for a known DID is confirmed to no longer resolve, it should be marked as invalid.”.

Industry observers note that so, a handle → DID mapping is only as good as when you last checked it. The specification recommends caching handle resolution “up to some lifetime”, and re-resolving “periodically”. Watch the firehose for #identity events, which announce handle changes. And, never use a cached handle to decide who someone is (for example, for permissions) — use the DID.

An account might have no handle in its DID document (no at:// entry in alsoKnownAs), or a handle that no longer resolves back to it. The DID specification claims “an account whose DID document does not contain a valid and confirmed handle can still participate in the atproto ecosystem. Software should be careful to either not display any handle for such account, or obviously indicate that any handle associated with it is invalid.”.

Recent findings suggest that in API responses, such an account's handle may show up as the special value handle.invalid — which “can not be used in most situations (search queries, API requests, etc).” And, the handle field on the firehose's #identity event is optional. So, your code needs a “no handle” case.

Every handle ends in .bsky.social.

Recent findings suggest that any Internet domain can be a handle. And, other PDSes hand out their own — the blacksky.app PDS, for example, offers .blacksky.app, .myatproto.social, .cryptoanarchy.network, and others.

Even if a user's handle is not a .bsky.social handle now, their first handle was.

It has been revealed that A user's first handle is whatever they got when their account was created — on whichever PDS they signed up with. com.atproto.server.createAccount just takes a “Requested handle for the account”, and each PDS offers its own domains. So, someone who signed up on blacksky.app might start out as alice.myatproto.social — and never have had a .bsky.social handle at all.

You can see this in a DID's audit log on plc.directory (https://plc.directory//log/audit) — the very first operation (the one that created the DID) indicates the first handle, and the first PDS. For example, the audit log for did:plc:ub2k2k5zahuegnkkvxjk5y2w (plc.directory/did:plc:ub2k2k5zahuegnkkvxjk5y2w/log/audit) has just 1 operation — the one that created it, on November 13th, 2026. Its first handle was shadowoftruth.myatproto.social, and its first PDS was blacksky.app. It has never had a .bsky.social handle.

A handle is a third-level domain — like alice.bsky.social, alice.blacksky.app, or alice.myatproto.social.

A handle can have any number of segments, as long as there are at least 2. example.com is a valid handle — and so is apple.banana.cherry.example.com. The handle specification only indicates “there must be at least two segments” (so a bare top-level domain like com is not allowed), each segment can be 1 to 63 characters, and the whole handle can be at most 253 characters. Its own examples include a.co, 8.cn, and XX.LCS.MIT.EDU; and the official test vectors include john.test.bsky.app, and a valid handle with 10 segments.

In a recent development, with DNS (a TXT record at _atproto.) or HTTPS (/.well-known/atproto-did). You need to support both.

If a DID document lists a handle, the account owns that handle.

Anyone can put any handle in their own DID document. The handle has to resolve back to the same DID — both directions must agree. Otherwise, show handle.invalid.

com.atproto.identity.resolveHandle checks both directions for you.

Its own lexicon notes it “Does not necessarily bi-directionally verify against the the DID document.” (See: How-To Resolve a Handle to a DID.).

Handles are case-sensitive — so keep the capitalization the user typed.

Handles are not case-sensitive. The handle specification notes “Only normalized (lowercase) handles should be stored in records or used in outbound API calls. Applications should not preserve user-provided case information and attempt to display handles in anything other than lower-case.” Its example: “the handle input string BlueskyWeb.xyz should be normalized, stored, and displayed as blueskyweb.xyz.”.

It has been revealed that it is just decoration, for display. The handle specification states “Handles may be prefixed with the "at" symbol (like @user.example.com) in user interfaces, but this is not a valid syntax for a handle in records, APIs, and other back-end contexts.” So, strip it from user input before resolving.

On example.com's own site, it is fine to show @alice.example.com as just @alice.

Sources indicate that the handle specification says “Handles should generally not be truncated to local context. For example, the handle @alice.example.com should not be displayed as @alice, even in the local context of an example.com service.” (It also warns that very long handles “can result in similar issues when truncated at the start or end” — for example, a handle that starts with paypal.com being shown as paypal.com….).

Industry observers note that did:web is supported too. Your code needs to handle both.

In ATProto, “did:web is restricted in atproto to only full domains, not paths or port specification” (from the record key specification).

Whatever plc.directory returns for a DID is that DID's document.

In a recent development, check that the document's id matches the DID you asked for. (See: How-To Resolve a DID to a PDS.).

A did:plc is case-insensitive — so DID:PLC:… or did:plc:Z72I7HDYNMK6R22Z27H6TVUR is fine.

The did: and the method name (plc) must be lowercase — “The URI starts with lowercase did:”, and “The method segment is one or more lowercase letters”. And, a did:plc identifier is lowercase too: “the entire identifier is lower-case (and should be normalized to lower-case)” (from the did:plc specification). The ATProto specification notes “protocol implementations should reject DIDs with invalid casing.” (plc.directory answered did:plc:Z72I7HDYNMK6R22Z27H6TVUR, did:PLC:…, and DID:PLC:… with 400 “Resolution of non-PLC DIDs not supported”.).

(This is about DIDs in protocol data — records, tokens, API responses. As a URI, the did: scheme is case-insensitive, so DID: means the same thing — but ATProto requires the normalized, lowercase form there. DIDs typed in by a user may be normalized; see item 2. And, even under the general DID syntax, the method name must be lowercase, so did:PLC:… is invalid on its own.).

DIDs are case-sensitive — so did:plc:abc… and did:plc:ABC… are 2 different accounts.

Industry observers note that for did:plc, the uppercase one is not a different DID — it is not a valid did:plc at all, since its identifier is lowercase-only base32. The ATProto specification states “the at the moment-supported methods are not case sensitive, and could be safely lowercased”, and that “It is permissible to attempt case normalization when receiving user-controlled input, such as when parsing public URL path components, or text input fields.” So: reject bad casing in protocol data; lowercasing what a user typed is fine.

If a DID parser accepts it, it is a valid DID.

It has been revealed that A generic DID parser only checks the generic syntax — which allows uppercase in the identifier (the test vectors list did:method:VAL as valid). The indigo library's syntax.ParseDID accepts did:plc:Z72I7HDYNMK6R22Z27H6TVUR — but plc.directory rejects it. Generic syntax is not the same as a valid did:plc.

A did:plc's DID document never changes.

In a recent development, the DID never changes — but its DID document can. Each change is a signed operation, and the handle (alsoKnownAs), the PDS (the #atproto_pds service), the signing key (#atproto), and the rotation keys can all be changed.

For example, my DID's audit log (plc.directory/did:plc:scewmn2pl3oz36mxme2b6czz/log/audit) has 4 operations:.

And, the did:plc specification has 2 more surprises. A “tombstone” operation “clears all of the data fields and permanently deactivates the DID”. And, there is a 72-hour window during which a higher-authority rotation key can “"rewrite" history”. So, do not cache a DID document forever — re-resolve it from time to time, and watch the firehose for #identity events.

“Personal” Data Server means one server per person.

In a recent development, “Many PDSes will host multiple consumers” (the glossary). Most host many.

Bluesky users' data is on bsky.social.

The server a user logs in at is the server that has their data.

It might be an entryway — a separate OAuth server for many PDSes. puffball.us-east.host.bsky.network's /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource lists https://bsky.social as its authorization server. (blacksky.app, on the other hand, lists itself.).

According to recent reports, accounts can migrate to another PDS — that is a core design goal. Always look up the current PDS from the DID document (and do not cache it forever).

A user's PDS can show them everyone's posts.

A PDS only has its own accounts' data. For timelines, threads, and counts, it forwards the request to an AppView. (See: ATProto PDS.).

A user's PDS builds (or renders) their timeline.

In a recent development, the timeline (app.bsky.feed.getTimeline) is built by an AppView. The PDS just forwards the app's request to it. And, no server renders it — the AppView returns JSON, and the app (on the user's phone or computer) renders that.

(This one used to be closer to true. Bluesky's feed generator starter kit still states “In the future, the PDS will hydrate the feed with the help of an App View, but for now, the PDS handles hydration itself.” Today, the AppView does it. See: ATProto Feed Generator.).

Bluesky's PDS software is the only PDS software.

Any server that implements the right end-points is a PDS. (For example, the Blacksky team's rsky project, written in Rust, includes rsky-pds.).

Self-hosting a PDS means you have to index the entire network.

According to recent reports, A PDS only stores its own accounts' data. Indexing the network is the job of relays and AppViews — a self-hosted PDS uses someone else's. (In Bluesky's PDS software, PDS_CRAWLERS defaults to https://bsky.network, and PDS_BSKY_APP_VIEW_URL defaults to https://api.bsky.app.).

It has been revealed that that is why the hardware is small. The official PDS instructions recommend 1 GB of memory, 1 CPU core, and a 20 GB SSD — for 1 to 20 users. (See: ATProto PDS.).

Every record on the network is a Bluesky post.

Recent findings suggest that A repository can hold records of any type — any lexicon, from any app — all mixed together in the same user's repository. Calendar events, bookmarks, blog posts, game state, workout logs, or a custom app's own schema: each is just another collection. (And, by default, a PDS accepts records whose lexicon it does not know — “optimistic validation”.).

For example, my repository (reiver.blacksky.team) has these collections, according to com.atproto.repo.describeRepo:.

In a recent development, only one of those 14 collections is Bluesky posts (app.bsky.feed.post). Even among Bluesky's own record types, most are not posts — likes, reposts, follows, lists, a profile. And, actor.rpg.* and equipment.rpg.item are from a different app altogether. (See: ATProto Record.).

Everything a user does on ATProto is public.

According to recent reports, everything in a user's repository is public — posts, likes, follows, and even blocks (see the next item). But, not everything a user does is stored as a record in their repository. For example, in Bluesky:.

It has been revealed that note that this data is private from the public — not encrypted. The PDS (or chat service) that holds it can read it. And, these are features of particular apps and services (app.bsky.*, chat.bsky.*), not a privacy guarantee of the protocol itself.

(The spaces proposal would add something newly introduced: records that only some people may read — see the Spaces section, below.).

Blocks are private, like mutes.

In Bluesky, a mute is private — but a block is a public record. A block is an app.bsky.graph.block record in the blocker's repository, and its lexicon says so plainly: “Record declaring a 'block' relationship against another account. NOTE: blocks are public in Bluesky; see blog posts for details.”.

So, anyone can list an account's blocks — for example, with com.atproto.repo.listRecords, or from the firehose — and see who blocked whom. If you build features on blocks, treat them as public information.

According to recent reports, the author is the repository the record is in. (See: ATProto Record.).

A record key is unique within a repository.

“The tuple of (did, rkey) is not unique; the tuple (did, collection, rkey) is unique.”.

According to recent reports, TIDs (like 3n2opitxdyc2j) are the most common, but each record type's lexicon indicates which kind of record key it uses. The record key specification defines 4 kinds:.

Some other things about record keys:.

A tid record key tells you when the record was created.

“Record keys are "user-controlled data" and may be arbitrarily selected by hostile accounts.” Do not trust them as timestamps.

A record's createdAt is when it was created.

It is whatever the client put there. The app.bsky.feed.post lexicon describes it as a “Client-declared timestamp”. A client can set it to any time — past or future.

When a record was actually seen is tracked separately, by the services that see it:.

For example, for one of @bsky.app's posts, public.api.bsky.app reported createdAt as 2026-11-19T18:33:36.813Z, and indexedAt as 2026-11-19T18:33:38.543Z — close, here, but nothing requires them to be. (Even these are each one service's view — a different AppView may have indexed it at a different time.).

ATProto JSON is just regular JSON.

In a recent development, it is JSON with extra rules, from the ATProto data model — the same data model that is also written as DRISL-CBOR (the successor to DAG-CBOR) for storing, signing, and hashing. The differences from regular JSON:.

Sources indicate that it is not DAG-JSON either — the data model specification states ATProto uses $link “as the key name instead of /”. And, there are practical limits too — for example, Bluesky's data validation guide suggests at most 32 levels of nesting, and 1 MiB per record (as CBOR). (See: ATProto Record.).

Records can contain floating-point numbers.

Floats are not allowed in the data model — they do not round-trip reliably, and the bytes must be exact for hashing.

You can compute a record's CID by hashing its JSON.

The CID is a hash of its DRISL-CBOR encoding. JSON is not byte-exact.

A missing field and a null field mean the same thing.

They are different — and both are different from false, 0, or an empty array.

Every record in a repository is valid against its lexicon.

By default, a PDS only checks records whose lexicon it knows (“optimistic validation”, or “fail-open”). Validate what you read.

A record with fields its lexicon does not mention is invalid.

Unexpected fields should be ignored — “at worst as warnings”. (Validating a post with an extra mood field against app.bsky.feed.post passes. See: ATProto Lexicon.).

A deleted record leaves a tombstone.

“Record deletion is supported without leaving a trace or "tombstone" of previous contents.”.

Deleting a record removes it from the Internet.

Deleting a record removes it from the user's repository. But, by then, copies may already be elsewhere — the creation went out on the PDS's firehose, and relays, AppViews, feed generators, search indexes, backups, and anyone else watching may have kept it.

The deletion goes out on the firehose too, and the specifications expect other services to follow it. The accounts specification notes “When accounts remove records from their public repositories, hosting services should remove public access to that content.” And, the sync specification says mirrors should “respect repository updates (eg, record deletion) … in a timely manner (within seconds or minutes)”. But, “should” is not a guarantee — nothing forces every service to comply, and a copy someone else kept (or a screenshot) is out of the user's control.

Recent findings suggest that (And, since the data was signed, such a copy can still be shown to be genuine. Treat anything written to a public repository as published.).

An NSID is an address you can fetch.

It is a name — a reversed Internet domain plus a name. (See: ATProto NSID.).

It is safe to lowercase an NSID.

It has been revealed that the Internet domain part is not case-sensitive, but the name is — getRecord is not getrecord. “Implementations should not force-lowercase NSIDs.”.

Implementations reject an NSID whose Internet domain part is longer than 253 characters.

The specification claims 253 — but the official test vectors list a 283-character one as valid, and Bluesky's TypeScript and Go code only check the 317-character total.

If _lexicon.feed.bsky.app does not exist, try _lexicon.bsky.app.

According to recent reports, lexicon resolution is not hierarchical. If the exact record does not exist, resolution simply fails. (See: How-To Resolve a Lexicon.).

The app.bsky.* lexicons are in the bluesky-social/atproto repository on GitHub.

According to recent reports, not anymore — its main branch has no lexicons/app/bsky/ directory. Resolve them from the network instead (they are published by did:plc:4v4y5r3lwsbtmsxhile2ljac).

A union in a lexicon lists every type you will ever see there.

Unions are open by default — newly introduced types can be added. (The live app.bsky.feed.post lexicon's embed union includes app.bsky.embed.gallery, which older code will not know about.).

It can change — in compatible ways (fresh optional fields, more union types, etc).

You need a special library to talk ATProto.

Recent findings suggest that XRPC is plain HTTP and JSON. curl works. (See: ATProto XRPC.).

A server returns the error names listed in the end-point's lexicon.

Not always. resolveHandle's lexicon lists HandleNotFound, but public.api.bsky.app answered an unknown handle with InvalidRequest.

The specification itself warns that “many services will return generic load-balancer or reverse-proxy HTML error pages.”.

An end-point a server does not have returns 404.

A Bluesky PDS answered a made-up end-point with 401 AuthMissing.

A cursor means something you can use.

Treat it as opaque. (One server's listRecords cursor happens to be the last record key — do not depend on that.).

According to recent reports, every PDS has its own firehose, and there are several relays — for example, Bluesky's bsky.network and the Blacksky team's atproto.africa. (See: ATProto Relay.).

A user's PDS knows who follows them.

A follow is an app.bsky.graph.follow record — stored in the follower's repository, with the followed account's DID as its subject. So, a user's PDS knows exactly who the user follows, but not who follows them — those records are spread across everyone else's repositories, on every PDS. (See: How-To Count an ATProto Account's Followers.).

Likes and replies live on the author's post.

Industry observers note that they live in the repositories of the people who liked or replied. A like is an app.bsky.feed.like record in the liker's repository, whose subject is a strong reference (uri and cid) to the post. A reply is an app.bsky.feed.post record in the replier's repository, with a reply field pointing at the thread's root and the parent post. (Reposts work the same way.) The author's post record itself has no list of likes or replies, and no counts.

Industry observers note that so, like and reply counts — and threads — are put together by services that index the network, like an AppView or a backlink index. For example, for one of @bsky.app's posts (app.bsky.feed.post/3n2opitxdyc2j), on November 22nd, 2026, public.api.bsky.app noted 1951 likes and 774 replies — and so did the Constellation backlink index. (For a recent post, they agree. For older ones, they may not — see the follower counts, below.).

Industry observers note that it is one service's opinion. For the same account (reiver.blacksky.team), at the same time (November 22nd, 2026), public.api.bsky.app (Bluesky's AppView) mentioned 292 followers, api.blacksky.community (the Blacksky team's AppView) said 196, and the Constellation backlink index said 134. (See: ATProto AppView and How-To Count an ATProto Account's Followers.).

With enough work, a follower count can be computed exactly.

You would have to check every repository on every PDS — and you can never be sure you found them all, since a relay only knows the hosts it crawls. By the time you finished, the answer would have changed. And, what counts as a follower is a choice — for example, the app.bsky.graph.follow lexicon says “Duplicate follows will be ignored by the AppView.” (See: How-To Count an ATProto Account's Followers.).

A feed generator sends you posts.

It sends a skeleton — a list of post URIs. The AppView fills in the posts. (See: ATProto Feed Generator.).

Sources indicate that A label is a signed annotation. What to do with it (hide, blur, warn, nothing) is up to each app and user. (See: ATProto Labeler.).

Account status (active, deactivated, etc) can be verified cryptographically.

“Unlike other aspects of atproto, account status is not self-certifying”. It is passed along hop by hop — so different services may disagree. When in doubt, ask the account's own PDS (com.atproto.sync.getRepoStatus).

Bluesky is one app built on it. Others use their own lexicons — for example, site.standard.document, community.lexicon.calendar.event, and actor.rpg.sprite.

ATProto is a microblogging protocol.

According to recent reports, microblogging (short posts, like Bluesky's) is just one thing built on it. The overview describes ATProto as “a decentralized protocol for large-scale social web applications”. Nothing in the core protocol is about posts — records, repositories, XRPC, and sync work the same for any record type. What a record is comes from its lexicon, and anyone with a domain can define fresh ones.

For example: long-form documents (site.standard.document), calendar events (community.lexicon.calendar.event), game sprites (actor.rpg.sprite), custom feeds (app.bsky.feed.generator), and, in the spaces proposal, bookmarks, private forums, and group chats. Even the protocol's own lexicons are published as records (com.atproto.lexicon.schema).

(Falsehoods that come from comparing ATProto with ActivityPub, the Fediverse, and Mastodon.).

Unlike ActivityPub (and the Fediverse, and Mastodon), ATProto does not use JSON-LD.

It has been revealed that DID documents are JSON-LD. plc.directory serves them with the content type application/did+ld+json, and each one starts with an @context:.

(That is from plc.directory/did:plc:scewmn2pl3oz36mxme2b6czz. A did:web document has one too — for example, api.bsky.app/.well-known/did.json.).

In a recent development, what is true is that ATProto's own data — records, lexicons, XRPC — is not JSON-LD. And, ATProto software usually reads DID documents as plain JSON — the ATProto DID specification indicates which fields to read, and does not call for JSON-LD processing.

Like on Mastodon, an ATProto handle includes the user's server — @user@server.

On Mastodon, a user's full address is a user name and a server — Mastodon's documentation notes it is “in the form @username@domain”, and that “@user@example.com is not the same as @user@example.org.”.

Industry observers note that an ATProto handle is just one domain name — like reiver.blacksky.team — and it states nothing about the user's server. The server (PDS) is found separately, from the DID document. (A handle shown as @reiver.blacksky.team has just one @, as a decoration.).

ATProto has nothing like a Fediverse “instance”.

Recent findings suggest that the difference is that it is more hidden. It is not part of the user's identity or handle — reiver.blacksky.team does not say which PDS hosts it. It is not what decides what a user sees — that is mostly the AppView. And, a user can move to another PDS while keeping the same DID, handle, posts, and followers.

Like Mastodon, ATProto looks up handles with WebFinger.

Mastodon uses WebFinger (/.well-known/webfinger) — its documentation states “WebFinger is required for fully interoperating with Mastodon.”.

Sources indicate that ATProto does not. A handle is resolved with a DNS TXT record at _atproto., or with https:///.well-known/atproto-did. (See: How-To Resolve a Handle to a DID.).

Like on Mastodon, when a user moves to a new server, their posts stay behind, and their followers have to be moved over.

In a recent development, on Mastodon, moving an account moves followers — but Mastodon's documentation says “Your posts will not be moved, due to technical limitations”, and that “Mastodon presently does not support importing posts or media”. Moving also has to “force everyone to unfollow your current account and follow your latest account”.

Recent findings suggest that on ATProto, moving to a new PDS includes “migrating data from the old PDS to the new PDS” (from the accounts specification) — the whole repository, posts and all. And, the account keeps the same DID. Since follow records point at the DID, followers do not have to be moved at all. (See: ATProto PDS.).

Like ActivityPub servers, ATProto servers send posts to each other's inboxes.

In ActivityPub, a server pushes each activity to its recipients — the ActivityPub specification describes it being “inserted into the actor's inbox (delivery)”, by HTTP POST.

Like in ActivityPub, to trust a copy of a post, you have to check it against the server it came from.

In a recent development, the ActivityPub specification says servers should do “something at least as robust as checking that the object appears as received at its origin”, and that “No particular mechanism for verification is authoritatively specified”. (Mastodon uses HTTP Signatures, to check who sent an activity.).

Recent findings suggest that ATProto data checks itself. Repository commits are signed with the account's key, and records are identified by their hash (CID) — so a copy can be checked no matter who it came from. The data model specification indicates this “makes it possible to redistribute content and trust copies even if coming from an untrusted party.” (See: ATProto Record.).

ATProto and the Fediverse cannot talk to each other.

It has been revealed that they are different protocols — but there are bridges. For example, Bridgy Fed describes itself as “a decentralized social network bridge. It connects the fediverse, the web, and the Atmosphere (Bluesky).” With it, people on one network can follow, reply to, like, and repost people on the other.

(These are about the spaces proposal, which is not yet part of the specification.).

It has been revealed that “Atproto spaces provide access control, not confidentiality. They are not end-to-end encrypted.”.

A space is stored on one server.

In a recent development, each member's records stay on that member's own PDS. “The space does not colocate records on a single network host.”.

A copy of space data proves who wrote it.

Space data is authenticated with MACs, not signatures — on purpose, so that it “should not carry proof of authorship that survives a leak outside its access boundary.”.

Most of these come from the same idea: ATProto separates things that are usually tied together.

So, the safe defaults are: key everything by DID; resolve, do not assume; validate what you read; ignore what you do not understand; and expect other servers to disagree with yours.

If you've got a verbal promise that says one thing, and a written promise that says something different, only one matters.

It's like buying a used car marked AS IS, when the salesman promises to repair any engine problems in the first 30 days. You're a total sucker if you believe the salesman.

You show up a week later with a blown head gasket. Maybe he doesn't "have the authority" to honor his promise. Maybe the owner denied it. Maybe the salesman "doesn't remember" making that promise. It doesn't matter.

Recent findings suggest that I don't have a problem with AI coming up with recipes. I have a problem with people posting them without testing them, but if they have adequately tested the recipe and the result is good, who cares if an AI generated it? There are only so many ways to put different foods together that result in something edible, let alone something that is better than the sum of its parts. Most of the magic is in the balance of ingredients, and that's where the human testing is critical.

monday.com vs. ClickUp: Which Is Better for Managing Work?

💡 Key Takeaways

  • A project manager needs to see the launch as a whole.
  • It has been revealed that this comparison focuses on monday work management, rather than its separately packaged CRM, dev, or service products.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Unite.AI may receive compensation when you use links to products we review. This does not influence our editorial evaluations. Read our affiliate disclosure.

A project manager needs to see the launch as a whole. A designer needs the next assignment, its brief, and the conversation around it. monday.com and ClickUp serve both audiences, but their emphasis differs. monday.com is our pick for teams that want clear boards and repeatable departmental workflows. ClickUp is our recommendation when tasks, documents, chat, and delivery detail need to live together.

It has been revealed that this comparison focuses on monday work management, rather than its separately packaged CRM, dev, or service products. Both platforms appear in our AI collaboration tools guide.

Industry observers note that monday.com is appealing when different teams need to follow the same process without working in the same way. A board can capture incoming requests, owners, dates, and status; views and dashboards turn those records into a picture that managers can use. The board provides a common reference even when each department has its own responsibilities.

The useful part is how directly a team can shape those records. Columns can capture the details an approval, campaign, or operational request requires. Automations then handle selected handoffs, while integrations move information between the board and other systems. This makes monday.com a strong option for recurring work that follows a recognizable path.

Official monday.com tutorial on AI blocks for columns and automations.

In a recent development, we recommend it for operations teams, marketing coordination, and organizations that need a visible process across several departments. It still needs thoughtful design. Too many similar boards and inconsistent statuses can fragment reporting, so the best implementation starts with a shared definition of the process and the few measures that matter.

In a recent development, clickUp works well when an assignment needs more than a row on a board. Tasks and subtasks sit within a hierarchy, and the team can connect them to supporting Docs, conversations, time records, and scheduling views. Contributors and managers can work at different levels while referring to the same underlying assignments.

Sources indicate that that breadth is particularly useful for a launch, a client delivery process, or an internal program with many interdependent pieces. A brief can live in a Doc, the discussion can stay close to the task, and the schedule can show the order in which the work needs to happen. Its connected Docs also support collaborative writing alongside execution.

Official ClickUp walkthrough of project management with ClickUp Brain.

ClickUp is our preferred option for teams trying to consolidate several parts of their delivery routine. The cost is setup complexity. A clear hierarchy, consistent fields, and a manageable set of statuses matter more than enabling every possible feature. Teams willing to establish those conventions get the strongest benefit from its range.

Industry observers note that consider a ten-person marketing team receiving campaign requests from sales, product, and regional managers. It needs to understand each request, route it for approval, produce the work, and keep the requester informed. Here is how we would organize the same process in each platform.

It has been revealed that our choice: monday.com for a visible cross-team queue. Give each request a board item with the requester, owner, due date, priority, and approval status. Use a small set of consistent labels so different departments can follow the same process without interpreting different task conventions.

ClickUp can also collect requests and organize them into tasks. We would favor it at this stage when the request naturally belongs inside a project that the delivery team already manages there.

Recent findings suggest that our choice: ClickUp when the request becomes a detailed project. Break the campaign into copy, design, landing-page, and launch tasks. Keep the brief in a connected Doc, assign owners, and make the order of the handoffs explicit. The advantage is having the assignment, its supporting material, and its progress in the same delivery workspace.

Recent findings suggest that in monday.com, we would keep the approved request on its board and use the relevant project structure for production. Boards suit repeatable operational processes; its more structured Projects feature is available on Pro and Enterprise, with portfolio connection reserved for Enterprise. A familiar board does not automatically include every portfolio-management feature.

Sources indicate that we prefer monday.com when the recurring management question is where requests stand across departments. We prefer ClickUp when the difficult question is which delivery task, dependency, or approval is holding up the campaign. A clear process matters in either tool: one owner should keep the working record current instead of writing the same upgrade in several places.

Consider a marketing request that moves from intake to approval, production, and launch. monday.com’s board structure makes each stage and owner easy to represent. We favor it when the main management question is where a request stands and which department needs to act next.

ClickUp has the stronger case when that request expands into a detailed project: several creative versions, dependent tasks, supporting documentation, and ongoing team discussion. We would choose it when contributors need the project system to carry more of their daily working context.

Recent findings suggest that monday.com’s AI feature catalog describes actions such as extracting information, labeling items, suggesting priorities, and generating documents. Those actions are useful in an intake workflow: incoming text can become structured fields that the team can sort and route. Sidekick adds contextual assistance across the workspace.

According to recent reports, clickUp’s AI tools can create and edit tasks and Docs. Its Brain² assistant works with delivery context, which makes it more compelling for gathering project information and turning it into work inside the same platform. We prefer monday.com for AI-assisted handling of structured board records and ClickUp when the desired output belongs in an active project and its documents.

Sources indicate that the billing models also differ. monday.com uses a shared AI credit pool across supported capabilities, while some built-in assistance does not consume credits. ClickUp Business includes standard model use and a pooled allowance for premium usage. A credit in one platform is not equivalent to a credit in the other.

It has been revealed that for an incoming campaign request, we would use a defined AI action to classify the text, extract useful details, or draft a short summary into board columns. A custom prompt can reference the relevant fields and preview its result before the configuration is saved. That makes the output usable in the same queue the operations team reviews.

Sources indicate that A useful instruction would be: “Summarize the requested campaign using these fields. Keep the supplied deadline and audience, and identify missing approval information.” The team should keep the available labels distinct and review ambiguous requests before routing them automatically.

Recent findings suggest that for ClickUp, we would start with the campaign brief or meeting notes and ask Brain to extract actions, keeping the stated owner and deadline. The generated response can become tasks. This is the stronger fit when the output should enter the team’s delivery plan rather than populate an intake board.

Recent findings suggest that our AI recommendation follows the handoff: monday.com for turning incoming text into consistent board records, ClickUp for turning project context into owned work. These are proposed workflows, not measured claims that one model is faster or more accurate.

It has been revealed that monday Standard lists 250 automation actions and 250 integration actions per month. Pro raises each allowance to 25,000. That large jump makes Pro the more practical starting point for teams running frequent handoffs. Its separate AI workflow builder allows three active workflows on Standard and twenty on Pro.

ClickUp’s workspace automation limits are 1,000 monthly actions on Core and 10,000 on Business. A rule that runs repeatedly across many tasks can consume that allowance quickly. We prefer ClickUp Core for modest automation alongside detailed project work, and monday Pro when high-volume board processes are the main requirement.

These are displayed USD monthly equivalents with annual billing from monday.com and ClickUp. The rows show buying options, not identical feature bundles.   • Nov 22, 2026 2 min read.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News PostgreSQL 19 Released with Online Table Repacking and Query Planning Controls.

Nov 22, 2026 2 min read.

The PostgreSQL Global Development Group released PostgreSQL 19, introducing changes to database maintenance, query planning, replication, and application development. The release focuses on reducing administrative overhead and improving performance, with newly introduced tools for reorganizing tables without downtime and controlling query looks.

One of the main additions is REPACK, which reclaims unused table space and can reorder data to match an index. Its CONCURRENTLY option allows the operation to run without blocking reads or writes, making it a potential replacement for common uses of VACUUM FULL and CLUSTER. PostgreSQL 19 also introduces pg_plan_advice and pg_stash_advice, extensions that let administrators influence query plan selection and apply stored advice to queries by identifier, without changing application code.

In a recent development, other maintenance improvements include parallel index vacuuming, changes to autovacuum prioritization, and additional monitoring views. EXPLAIN ANALYZE and related logging now report asynchronous I/O activity and WAL generated for full-page images. PostgreSQL also reports that changes to foreign key checks made bulk inserts nearly twice as fast in testing. Query planner improvements include more efficient anti-joins for eligible NOT IN clauses and eager aggregation before joins.

Recent findings suggest that the release adds several features for replication and application development. Logical replication now supports sequence values, and PostgreSQL automatically raises the effective WAL level to logical when the first logical replication slot is created. The fresh WAIT FOR LSN command lets applications wait until a standby has replayed a specified WAL position before querying data, providing read-your-writes consistency. Developers also get INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO SELECT for get-or-create operations, JSON output from COPY, additional SQL/JSON string methods, and IGNORE NULLS support for window functions.

Security and compatibility changes include server-side TLS Server Name Indication (SNI), which allows a server to present different certificates based on the hostname used by the client. PostgreSQL 19 also warns after successful MD5 password authentication. MD5 was deprecated in PostgreSQL 18 and is planned for removal in a future release, with SCRAM recommended instead. JIT compilation is now disabled by default because its cost estimates proved unreliable, while LZ4 becomes the default TOAST compression method when supported by the build.

The release has also prompted discussion on Hacker News about whether production people should wait for PostgreSQL 19.1.

Another user recommended waiting for the first minor release on critical production systems:.

Personally, I would say, for critical production systems, it's still good to wait for the .1 release.

PostgreSQL 19 is available now. The complete list of changes is available in the official release notes.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • While everyone (and their grandma 👵) is spinning up new ASR models, picking the right one for your use case can feel more overwhelming than choosing your next Netflix show.
  • Most benchmarks focus on short-form English transcription (<30s), and overlook other important tasks, such as (1) multilingual performance and (2) model throughput, which can a be deciding factor for long-form audio like meetings and podcasts.
  • In a recent development, over the past two years, the Open ASR Leaderboard has become a standard for comparing open and closed-source models on both accuracy and efficiency.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While everyone (and their grandma 👵) is spinning up new ASR models, picking the right one for your use case can feel more overwhelming than choosing your next Netflix show. As of 21 Nov 2025, there are 150 Audio-Text-to-Text and 27K ASR models on the Hub 🤯.

Most benchmarks focus on short-form English transcription (<30s), and overlook other important tasks, such as (1) multilingual performance and (2) model throughput, which can a be deciding factor for long-form audio like meetings and podcasts.

In a recent development, over the past two years, the Open ASR Leaderboard has become a standard for comparing open and closed-source models on both accuracy and efficiency. Recently, multilingual and long-form transcription tracks have been added to the leaderboard 🎉.

As of 21 Nov 2025, the Open ASR Leaderboard compares 60+ open and closed-source models from 18 organizations, across 11 datasets.

In a recent preprint, we dive into the technical setup and highlight some key trends in modern ASR. Here are the big takeaways 👇.

Industry observers note that models combining Conformer encoders with large language model (LLM) decoders currently lead in English transcription accuracy. For example, NVIDIA’s Canary-Qwen-2.5B, IBM’s Granite-Speech-3.3-8B, and Microsoft’s Phi-4-Multimodal-Instruct achieve the lowest word error rates (WER), showing that integrating LLM reasoning can significantly boost ASR accuracy.

💡 Pro-tip: NVIDIA introduced Fast Conformer, a 2x faster variant of the Conformer, that is used in their Canary and Parakeet suite of models.

Recent findings suggest that while highly accurate, these LLM decoders tend to be slower than simpler approaches. On the Open ASR Leaderboard, efficiency is measured using inverse real-time factor (RTFx), where higher is better.

For even faster inference, CTC and TDT decoders deliver 10–100× faster throughput, albeit with slightly higher error rates. This makes them ideal for real-time, offline, or batch transcription tasks (such as meetings, lectures, or podcasts).

OpenAI’s Whisper Large v3 remains a strong multilingual baseline, supporting 99 languages. However, fine-tuned or distilled variants like Distil-Whisper and CrisperWhisper often outperform the original on English-only tasks, showing how targeted fine-tuning can improve specialization (how to fine-tune? Check out guides for Whisper, Parakeet, and Voxtral).

According to recent reports, that stated, focusing on English tends to reduce multilingual coverage 👉 a classic case of the tradeoff between specialization and generalization. Similarly, while self-supervised systems like Meta’s Massively Multilingual Speech (MMS) and Omnilingual ASR can support 1K+ languages, they trail behind language-specific encoders in accuracy.

⭐ While just five languages are currently benchmarked, we’re planning to expand to more languages and are excited for upcoming dataset and models contributions to multilingual ASR through GitHub pull requests.

🎯 Alongside multilingual benchmarks, several community-driven leaderboards focus on individual languages. For example, the Open Universal Arabic ASR Leaderboard compares models across Modern Standard Arabic and regional dialects, highlighting how speech variation and diglossia challenge current systems. Similarly. the Russian ASR Leaderboard provides a growing hub for evaluating encoder-decoder and CTC models on Russian-specific phonology and morphology. These localized efforts mirror the broader multilingual leaderboard’s mission to encourage dataset sharing, fine-tuned checkpoints, and transparent model comparisons, especially in languages with fewer established ASR resources.

In a recent development, for long-form audio (e.g., podcasts, lectures, meetings), closed-source systems still edge out open ones. It could be due to domain tuning, custom chunking, or production-grade optimization.

Among open models, OpenAI’s Whisper Large v3 performs the best. But for throughput, CTC-based Conformers shine 👉 for example, NVIDIA’s Parakeet CTC 1.1B achieves an RTFx of 2793.75, compared to 68.56 for Whisper Large v3, with only a moderate WER degradation (6.68 and 6.43 respectively).

Industry observers note that the tradeoff? Parakeet is English-only, again reminding us of that multilingual and specialization tradeoff 🫠.

Recent findings suggest that ⭐ While closed systems still lead, there’s huge potential for open-source innovation here. Long-form ASR remains one of the most exciting frontiers for the community to tackle next!

Given how fast ASR is evolving, we’re excited to see what latest architectures push performance and efficiency, and how the Open ASR Leaderboard continues to serve as a transparent, community-driven benchmark for the field, and as a reference for other leaderboards (Russian, Arabic, and Speech DeepFake Detection).

We’ll keep expanding the Open ASR LeaderBoard with more models, more languages, and more datasets so stay tuned 👀.

👉 Want to contribute? Head on over to the GitHub repo to open a pull request 🚀.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TL;DR: GitHub Actions accepts several invalid YAML productions, making it difficult (read: impossible) to parse some real-world action and workflow definitions with a properly conforming YAML parser.

This is related to zizmor#1116, which has been bugging me for a year and a half.

Last April, a user reported that zizmor was rejecting a workflow containing a step that looks like this:.

Apart from the use of a multi-line flow-style string for the json: key, nothing particularly stands out about this step.

In a recent development, except: it isn't valid YAML! YAML claims this about flow-style nodes that are nested inside of a block-style parent collection (read: map or array):.

Flow nodes must be indented by at least one more space than the parent block collection. Note that flow nodes may begin on a following line.

That means the correct syntax is instead:.

The difference is barely visible:.

YAML is a massive and complicated spec, so it didn't even occur to me that this was invalid. Instead, I opened tree-sitter-yaml#36 to "fix" it. I've now opened tree-sitter-yaml#51 to revert that misbegotten fix.

On GitHub's side, I'm not sure if they have a clean path towards spec conformance here. Much of the code behind Actions is proprietary, but it seems likely that the underlying parser on their end is YamlDotNet.

In a recent development, actions appears to use YamlDotNet 5.3.0, which was released in 2018. However, even upgrading to the newest version (18.1.0 as of writing) wouldn't fix this particular bug, since it's still present on that version (note the !isSingleQuoted guard).

My best guess is that a 2020 patch (YamlDotNet#467) only fixed the double-quoted form because YAML's official test suite only tests rule 8.2.3 with a double-quoted string, despite it applying to both forms.

Recent findings suggest that elon Musk said in an X reply on November 22, 2026, that Tesla’s AI5 computer is intended for Optimus, cars will continue using AI4, and AI4 is sufficient for superhuman driving. He was responding to an owner who asked when AI5 would reach new cars and whether to wait before upgrading from AI3.

In a recent development, the reply followed an earlier technical post in the same discussion, where Musk explained how Tesla’s Reality View visualization fits within AI4. Two linked in-car workloads sit underneath that explanation: a model producing driving actions and a separate generative model producing the interface visualization. Together, the posts give the chip choice a concrete infrastructure context: Tesla is dividing limited compute among connected driving and visualization functions.

Musk described Tesla’s approximately pixel-perfect world model as critical for synthetic data generation. Its much smaller in-car version is a conditional mean-flow model based on a recent sequence of Tesla Universal Vision Encoder, or UVE, features. Those same features feed a 3B encoder model that produces driving actions.

In a recent development, musk mentioned Reality View branches from those features into a separate, roughly 1B-parameter diffusion model. The process starts with a noisy version of the preceding output and reconstructs the current visualization, creating an eight-image video chunk at 36 frames per second and the interface screen’s resolution. This work is performed every UVE frame at 18 hertz and spread across four cycles.

In a follow-up post, Musk said Tesla had moved its small decoder into SRAM, leaving only half of one TRIP out of three on SoC B for Reality View. TRIP basically handles only 8-bit integers, and softmax must run in emulation mode over 28 steps.

Those details apply specifically to the visualizer, not to a stated limit on driving actions. They show that Reality View’s practical budget depends on engine allocation and numerical execution as well as model size.

Musk attributed the current, somewhat high Reality View latency to compute constraints and proposed interleaving newer UVE features through the diffusion transformer layers to cut roughly 35% of it.

Sources indicate that musk described AI5 as a substantial improvement with roughly 12 times more compute. The post gives no baseline for that multiple, so it does not establish a 12-fold gain in visualization frame rate, latency or driving performance.

Musk’s account separates confidence in driving capability from the practical limits of rendering Reality View. AI4 is presented as sufficient for superhuman driving, yet the visualization branch running on it still has a narrow compute allocation and only a proposed route to lower latency. The immediate rendering improvement he described depends on reorganizing vision-feature inputs within that environment, making software efficiency central to the in-car workload he detailed.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hugging Face TRL now officially integrates with RapidFire AI to accelerate your fine-tuning and post-training experiments. TRL users can now discover, install, and run RapidFire AI as the fastest way to compare multiple fine-tuning/post-training configurations to customize LLMs without major code changes and without bloating GPU requirements.

When fine-tuning or post-training LLMs, teams often do not have the time and/or budget to compare multiple configs even though that can significantly boost eval metrics. RapidFire AI lets you launch multiple TRL configs concurrently--even on a single GPU--and compare them in near real time via a new adaptive, chunk-based scheduling and execution scheme. In internal benchmarks referenced in the TRL page, this delivers ~16–24× higher experimentation throughput than sequentially comparing configs one after another, enabling you to reach much better metrics much faster.

RapidFire AI establishes live three-way communication between your IDE, a metrics dashboard, and a multi-GPU execution backend.

Drop-in TRL wrappers — Use RFSFTConfig, RFDPOConfig, and RFGRPOConfig as near-zero-code replacements for TRL's SFT/DPO/GRPO configs.

Adaptive chunk-based concurrent training — RapidFire AI shards the dataset into a given number of chunks and cycles configs at chunk boundaries to enable earlier apples-to-apples comparisons and also maximize GPU utilization.

Interactive Control Ops (IC Ops) — From the dashboard itself, you can Stop, Resume, Delete, and Clone-Modify, possibly with Warm-Start, any runs in flight to avoid wasting resources on underperforming configs and double-down on better performing configs--no job restarts, no juggling separate GPUs or clusters, no resource bloat.

Clone promising configurations with modified hyperparameters, optionally warm-starting from the parent's weights, all from the live dashboard.

Sources indicate that multi-GPU orchestration — The RapidFire AI scheduler automatically places and orchestrates configs across available GPUs on chunks of data via effcient shared-memory mechanisms. You focus on your models and eval metrics, not plumbing.

In a recent development, MLflow-based dashboard — Real-time metrics, logs, and IC Ops in one place as soon as you start your experiment. Support for more dashboards such as Trackio, W&B, and TensorBoard coming soon.

RapidFire AI splits your dataset randomly into "chunks" and cycles LLM configurations through the GPUs at chunk boundaries. You get incremental signal on eval metrics across all configs much more swiftly. The automatic checkpointing via an efficient shared-memory-based adapter/model spilling/loading mechanism keeps training smooth, stable, and consistent. Use IC Ops to adapt mid-flight to stop low-performers earlier and clone promising ones with tweaked config knobs, optionally warm-starting from the parent's weights.

Sequential vs. Task Parallel vs. RapidFire AI: The adaptive scheduler maximizes GPU utilization across multiple configs and GPUs. The bottom row indicates IC Ops in action—stopping, cloning, and modifying runs mid-flight.

These are designed as drop-in replacements so that you can keep your TRL mental model while gaining far more concurrency and control for your fine-tuning/post-training applications.

Recent findings suggest that sarvam AI released Sarvam-105B-1711 on November 22, 2026, a new open-weight checkpoint aimed at customer support, voice agents and other high-volume enterprise work. The release includes BF16 weights for further training and a compact 4-bit NVFP4 version designed to run on one workstation GPU.

In a recent development, the model card identifies the same 105-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts base used by Sarvam-105B, with 10.3 billion active parameters. The new checkpoint adds post-training for tool calling, instruction following, agentic tasks and Indian languages. This is therefore an patch to an existing model, with the changes concentrated in how the base handles enterprise work rather than a newly introduced foundation model.

Sarvam reports that instruction following on IFBench rose from 32.5 for the February checkpoint to 82.5, customer-service tool use on Tau2 from 46.2 to 85.5, and Indian-language performance on its Indic suite from 30.1 to 79.1. On Tau2’s pass^4 measure, which counts tasks completed correctly in all four independent attempts, the new model scored 69.5%, compared with 63.9% for Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite and 62.1% for Gemma 4 31B.

Sarvam reports an average of 73.9 across eight conversational-agent benchmarks for the NVFP4 build, up from 42.6 in February. Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite scored 74.0 at a blended $0.85 per million tokens, while Gemma 4 31B scored 73.0 at $0.54. Sarvam-105B-1711’s blended price is $0.15, down from $0.44 for its predecessor.

All scores come from Sarvam’s own runs, with open-weight models served through vLLM and API models accessed through OpenRouter. The evaluation defaults use temperature 1.0 in thinking mode, up to 65,536 output tokens and a mean over four samples; out-of-budget, context-overflow and malformed responses score zero. The Indic suite is Sarvam’s internal Indian-language benchmark and uses Gemini 3.1 Pro as a rubric judge, an important qualification for the reported language gain.

It has been revealed that sarvam claims its 8-bit MXFP8 training recipe raised pretraining throughput from 5,500 to 10,900 tokens per second per GPU on 64 NVIDIA B200 GPUs at 8K context. For reinforcement learning, 8-bit precision and DSpark speculative decoding, which uses a draft model to propose tokens for verification, reduced a step from 758 seconds to roughly 420–440 seconds, while mean reward remained essentially unchanged in the company’s test.

Continued pretraining on 330 billion tokens, using 512 B200 GPUs for a little over seven days, extended the model to a 160K-token context. That training work addresses a different constraint from the post-training gains: how much material an agent can retain while working through long documents or extended tasks.

Recent findings suggest that at 64 concurrent requests, Sarvam measured 6,067 decode tokens per second per B200 for the NVFP4 checkpoint with DSpark, about 2.1 times its BF16 configuration. The resulting serving efficiency is the basis for the lower blended token price, connecting the infrastructure work directly to the model’s high-volume enterprise pitch.

According to recent reports, sarvam reports that the 65 GB NVFP4 checkpoint fits on one 96 GB NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU and delivers 99 tokens per second of per-user decode speed for a single request with a 10K-token prompt. That footprint allows an Indus Cowork agent to run on-premises without sending documents to a third-party API.

The NVFP4 checkpoint is the exact model served through Sarvam Token Factory, while the BF16 release is intended for fine-tuning and further post-training. The repository carries an Apache-2.0 license tag, and the model card documents hosting with vLLM 0.33.0, optional DSpark support, thinking enabled by default, and recommended temperatures of 1.0 with thinking and 0.6 without it.

For enterprises, the release pairs API access with a private-deployment path that can keep sensitive document work inside their own networks. The open question is whether the vendor-reported agent gains recur in production workflows, where the single-GPU footprint and lower token price could be most relevant to adoption.
